**The government gave this aeroplane an X number in 2021 and then spent nearly nineteen million dollars on it without once writing the number down.**

The federal award record carries 73 transactions against this aircraft, running from 21 February 2014 to 30 September 2025 and totalling 29,085,924.37 dollars \[[USAspending][ref_usaspending]\]. **Not one of them calls it the X-62A.** They call it VISTA, or the variable stability in-flight simulator, or the airframe \[[USAspending][ref_usaspending]\]. The designation was allocated on 14 June 2021, according to the register of designations allocated since August 1998 that Andreas Parsch compiles from data the Department of Defense has released \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\], and by the date of this article, 1,637 days later, the accounting system that pays for the aeroplane has still never used it.

**None of this argues that the designation is unimportant. It measures where a designation lives.** The register records it, the press releases use it, the school that flies the aeroplane is proud of it, and the contracting officers who buy its maintenance have no use for it at all \[[VISTA X-62 Advancing Autonomy and Changing the Face of Air Power, Lockheed Martin, 13 February 2023][ref_lm_press]\] \[[X-62A and NF-16D VISTA, GlobalSecurity.org][ref_gs_x62]\] \[[USAspending][ref_usaspending]\].

This is the sixty-third article in the [X-Planes series][related_post_a297_framing], following the [X-1][related_post_a298_bell_x1], the [X-2][related_post_a299_bell_x2], the The [previous article][related_post_a358_dynetics_x61_gremlins] established that the register stops being a primary source at the X-61A, because the compiler's note states that for allocations after October 2018 the official description is no longer releasable to the public and prints the reconstructed ones in blue \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\]. **This is the second article on the far side of that line and the finding holds.** Every register count in this article is taken from every row of the copy the compiler last updated on 23 August 2026. Of the 31 rows whose designation begins with the letter X, 21 carry official wording, 9 do not, and 1 is partly official, and this is one of the 9. That copy is later than this article's date. The version current on that date, the compiler's update of 11 August 2025 as the Internet Archive captured it on 6 December 2025, held 526 rows, twenty-nine of them X rows, and lacked fifteen later rows that include the X-68A and the X-76A \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum, 11 August 2025][ref_mds_addendum_2025]\]. Under that version the X rows divided into 21 with official wording, 8 without and none partly official, 25 of the twenty-nine carried an engines cell, and the medians were 110 characters across the X rows and 95 across the register. **The row's unofficial wording, its length rank, its verb and its engine are the same in both versions.**

The reconstruction reads as follows.

> *VISTA*; NF-16D redesignated after upgrade for "Skyborg" program

That is 62 characters including the popular name and 55 without it, against a median of 109 across the X rows and 92 across the whole register, each measured without the popular name and the compiler's note marker. **Only 2 of the 31 X rows carry a shorter one.**

### One Word in This Row Appears Nowhere Else in the Register

**The word `redesignated` appears in exactly 1 row of all 539, and this is it.**

The idea is not unique. 8 of the 31 X rows describe an aircraft modified from an existing one. **What is unique is the verb.** The other 7 say *highly modified*, or *converted*, or *derivative of*, or *upgrade*. **Only this one says the aeroplane was renamed.** That claim concerns paperwork where the others describe metal, and no other row in the register makes it.

**That is fitting, because the allocation accompanied an upgrade of the aeroplane's computers and software, and its airframe was left as it was.** The aeroplane had been flying as VISTA for 29.2 years when it became an X-plane. It was not built for the number, and the upgrade that accompanied the number replaced its simulation system and added a system for autonomous control of the simulation, with no rebuild of the airframe \[[X-62A and NF-16D VISTA, GlobalSecurity.org][ref_gs_x62]\].

## The Research Question

**The aeroplane is not the subject and an article that treated it as one would have nothing to say.**

The X-62A is a two-seat F-16D. Its span is the F-16's span, its wing area is the F-16's wing area, its engine is a production fighter engine, and its performance is tabulated in the ordinary reference works \[[General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon][ref_f16]\]. Nothing about the airframe is a research question and this article will not pretend otherwise.

**What is a research question is whether one aeroplane can be made to behave like a different aeroplane, closely enough that the pilot flying the first cannot tell it from the second.** That is a control problem, it has an exact statement, and it has an exact condition for solvability that was written down in a Technical Memorandum of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, abbreviated NASA, dated 18 October 1967, twenty-four years before this aeroplane first flew as VISTA \[[Erzberger, Analysis and Design of Model Following Control Systems by State Space Techniques, NASA Technical Memorandum X-61189, 18 October 1967][ref_erzberger_1967]\]. **The condition concerns the host aeroplane's controls and not its performance.** For that reason the vehicle drops out of the argument almost immediately, and this article spends its arithmetic on a matrix where a flight envelope might be expected.

The sections below establish four things. **The condition for exact model following is a subspace containment**, and it fixes how many independent controls an in-flight simulator needs and in which axes. **The determinant that decides whether those controls are independent is a distance**, being the separation between two surfaces measured in chords. **The frequency at which the simulation runs out of authority is published**, in a table of deflection and rate limits that NASA released in 1979, and for one surface it falls below a fighter's short period. And **an in-flight simulator cannot reproduce an aeroplane quicker than its hardware**, which makes the set of aeroplanes it can imitate one-sided in a way no amount of software will fix.

**The economics and the paperwork are read as evidence in themselves**, because the contract record for this aeroplane answers a question that neither of the previous two articles could ask. The X-60A's money and the X-61A's money paid for a development programme with a beginning and an end. **This money pays to keep one aeroplane flying**, in calendar-year increments, for a decade, and it therefore measures what an instrument of this kind costs to own.

## Programme Origin

**The aeroplane and its number have two different origins, twenty-nine years apart, and this section takes them in turn.** The aeroplane is a Block 30 F-16D modified to carry a second flight control system \[[X-62A and NF-16D VISTA, GlobalSecurity.org][ref_gs_x62]\], and it first flew in that modified form in April 1992 \[[General Dynamics X-62 VISTA][ref_x62_wikipedia]\], on 9 April by one account \[[Flight Test Files, Viper X, Vintage Aviation News][ref_vintage_viper_x]\]. No source consulted dates any flight of the production airframe before its modification, so every interval this article measures from April 1992 is measured from the first flight as VISTA. The number was allocated on 14 June 2021 \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\]. The four parts of this section read the name the government gives the aeroplane, the engine its register row names against the engine its block number implies, the status letter it carried before the X, and the interval between its first flight and its designation.

### The Name Does Not Spell Its Own Acronym

**VISTA has been expanded 7 different ways in the federal award record for this one aeroplane**, across 55 occurrences. The count covers the government's descriptions of its contracts \[[USAspending][ref_usaspending]\].

| Expansion | Occurrences | Keeps the word stability |
|---|---|---|
| Variable stability in-flight simulator and test aircraft | 23 | yes |
| Variable stability in-flight simulator | 21 | yes |
| Variable stability in-flight simulator test aircraft | 5 | yes |
| Variable in-flight stability test aircraft | 2 | yes |
| Variable stability inflight simulator test aircraft | 2 | yes |
| Variable in-flight simulator test aircraft | 1 | no |
| Variable stability in-flight test aircraft | 1 | yes |

**54 of the 55 keep the word `stability` and 1 drops it.** The contracting system is consistent about the one word and inconsistent about everything else, including whether the aeroplane is a simulator, a test aircraft, or both, and including where the hyphen goes.

**Now count the letters.** Variable, stability, in-flight, simulator, test, aircraft gives V, S, I, S, T, A. **The acronym is VISTA and the expansion spells VSISTA.** The word `stability`, which the award record preserves in 54 of 55 descriptions, contributes no letter at all. **In that expansion the S of stability is silent.**

**And the aeroplane's prime contractor has now fixed it.** Lockheed Martin's announcement of the artificial-intelligence flights writes the name as **Variable In-flight Simulation Test Aircraft** \[[VISTA X-62 Advancing Autonomy and Changing the Face of Air Power, Lockheed Martin, 13 February 2023][ref_lm_press]\], which does spell VISTA, letter for letter, with nothing left over. **The repair was made by deleting the word that never fitted.**

**The consequence is not cosmetic.** The original name says the aeroplane's variable quantity is its stability. The corrected name says the variable quantity is the simulation. **Those are different claims about what the machine is for**, and the second is the better description of an aeroplane that now spends its time hosting autonomous control software. The letters did not change. The subject did.

**The federal award record, which has not adopted the correction, is the largest body of text this article searched in which the older expansion still stands.** Whether the change of wording was a considered decision or an ordinary drift in a marketing department is not something the public record settles, and this article does not claim it was deliberate. **What is measured is that the two names differ, that the difference is exactly the word the acronym never contained, and that the money still uses the old one.**

### A Block Number That Means One Engine and a Cell That Names Another

**The engines cell is the one part of this register row not about simulation, and it contradicts the aeroplane's block number.**

The row reads `1 Pratt & Whitney F100` \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\]. 27 of the 31 X rows carry an engines cell at all, and this is the only one of them naming that engine.

**The aeroplane is a Block 30, and the Air Force's block convention gives a Block 30 a General Electric engine.** When the Alternate Fighter Engine programme brought a second supplier to the F-16 in the nineteen eighties, the two inlets and the two engines were distinguished by the last digit of the block number. **Blocks ending in zero take the General Electric F110 and blocks ending in two take the Pratt and Whitney F100** \[[General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon][ref_f16]\] \[[General Electric F110][ref_f110]\] \[[Pratt and Whitney F100][ref_f100]\]. A Block 30 with an F100 is, by that convention, a contradiction in terms.

**Both statements are true and the resolution is that the aeroplane was re-engined.** It flew its thrust-vectoring work behind a General Electric F110-GE-100 fitted with an axisymmetric vectoring exhaust nozzle, completing 95 test flights before that programme ended in 1994 \[[X-62 Variable-Stability In-Flight Test Aircraft, Air and Space Forces Magazine weapons and platforms entry][ref_afa_x62]\]. A Pratt and Whitney thrust-vectoring programme was planned next and was cancelled, **and the aeroplane was converted to a standard F100-PW-229 and returned to its operators in June 1997** \[[F-16 VISTA, MATV and NF-16D, Variable-stability In-flight Simulator Test Aircraft, F-16.net][ref_f16net_vista]\]. The trade press records the same engine in its data table \[[X-62 Variable-Stability In-Flight Test Aircraft, Air and Space Forces Magazine weapons and platforms entry][ref_afa_x62]\].

**So the register's engines cell is right and the block number is right, and the two disagree because the aeroplane outlived the convention that named it.** This article cannot say which inlet the aeroplane now carries, and the inlet is the part of an engine change that a block number encodes. The public record does not settle it.

**The rest of the airframe is assembled from three blocks as well.** The prime contractor describes it as a modified F-16D Block 30 Peace Marble Two aircraft upgraded with Block 40 avionics \[[VISTA X-62 Advancing Autonomy and Changing the Face of Air Power, Lockheed Martin, 13 February 2023][ref_lm_press]\], and the dorsal fairing that houses the variable-stability computers comes from the Israeli configuration, while the heavyweight landing gear is derived from the Block 40 and exists so that the aeroplane can simulate types with higher landing sink rates than an F-16 tolerates \[[General Dynamics X-62 VISTA][ref_x62_wikipedia]\].

**That last detail is the first sign of what this article is about.** A landing gear was changed not to improve the aeroplane but to widen the set of other aeroplanes it can pretend to be. **The modification is in the simulation's envelope rather than in the aircraft's.**

#### The Letter It Carried Before the X

**Before 2021 the aeroplane was an NF-16D, and the N is a status prefix with a precise meaning.** It denotes special test, permanent, and the prefix is applied when the modifications are so drastic that returning the aircraft to its original configuration, or converting it to a standard operational one, is beyond practicable or economic limits \[[X-62A and NF-16D VISTA, GlobalSecurity.org][ref_gs_x62]\] \[[Designations of U.S. Military Aircraft, including the modified mission and status prefix letters][ref_mds_aircraft]\].

**In-flight simulation at the two American test pilot schools was described in the open literature nine years before this aeroplane flew as VISTA** \[[Knotts and Parrag, In-Flight Simulation at the U.S. Air Force and Naval Test Pilot Schools, AIAA Flight Simulation Technologies Conference, 1983][ref_knotts_1983]\], and the school has continued to publish what it builds, including a ground-based handling-qualities simulator described by William Gray, whom the school's announcement of the redesignation names as the aeroplane's chief test pilot \[[X-62A and NF-16D VISTA, GlobalSecurity.org][ref_gs_x62]\], \[[Gray and Kemper, Creating an Aircraft Handling Qualities Simulator for the U.S. Air Force Test Pilot School, U.S. Air Force Test and Evaluation Days, 2009][ref_gray_2009]\] and the integration of uncrewed flight test into its curriculum by the authors of the papers on this aeroplane \[[Abdulrahim et al. 2025][ref_tps_uas_2025]\].

**The N is therefore a stronger statement about the aeroplane than the X is.** The X says the aircraft is used for research. **The N says it cannot practicably go back.** The aeroplane carried the stronger letter until 2021 and the weaker one for the last 4.48 years.

**And the X did not replace a claim about the aeroplane. It replaced a claim about its owner's intentions.** The school that operates it said at the time that the redesignation reflected the research done on the aircraft over nearly thirty years and acknowledged the upgrade programme then under way \[[X-62A and NF-16D VISTA, GlobalSecurity.org][ref_gs_x62]\]. **A redesignation that reflects the past is a different object from one that authorises a future**, and this series has met the second kind repeatedly and the first kind once.

### The Aeroplane Is Twenty-Nine Years Older Than Its Number

**The X-62A first flew as VISTA in April 1992 and was designated on 14 June 2021**, which from 9 April 1992 is 10,658 days, or 29.2 years \[[General Dynamics X-62 VISTA][ref_x62_wikipedia]\] \[[Flight Test Files, Viper X, Vintage Aviation News][ref_vintage_viper_x]\] \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\]. By the date of this article it has been flying as VISTA for 33.7 years and has carried an X number for 4.48 of them.

$$
F = \frac{T_n - T_d}{T_n - T_0}
\tag{1}
$$

**That fraction is 13.3 percent.** Seven-eighths of this aeroplane's flying life as VISTA happened before it was an X-plane, and it is still flying, so the fraction is still falling relative to what it would have been had the number come first.

**This series has now met five distinct orderings between a designation and the aeroplane it names**, and setting them beside one another is instructive because the register's chronology conceals all of them.

| Ordering | Case |
|---|---|
| The number comes first and the aeroplane follows | the [X-1][related_post_a298_bell_x1] and most of the early series |
| The number comes after the aeroplane has stopped flying | the [X-53][related_post_a350_boeing_x53] |
| The number is allocated and no aeroplane is ever built | the [X-54][related_post_a351_gulfstream_x54] |
| The number follows the first flight by months | the [X-55][related_post_a352_lockheed_martin_x55] |
| The number follows the first flight by three decades and the aeroplane is still flying | the X-62A |

**The fifth is the only one in which the designation describes a change of purpose rather than an event in the aeroplane's life.** Nothing happened to the metal in June 2021 that had not happened many times before. **What changed was the identity of the thing the machine was built to deceive**, and the register records that change in the one row of 539 that uses the word `redesignated`.

## What It Costs to Keep an Instrument Flying

**The previous two articles read a contract record that paid for a development programme. This one reads a contract record that pays rent on an aeroplane.**

The X-60A's money outlived its publicity by three years and ended by paying to ship equipment, as the [X-60 article][related_post_a357_generation_orbit_x60] reports. The X-61A's money stopped forty-seven days after the flight that mattered while the period of performance ran on for another four years, as the [X-61 article][related_post_a358_dynetics_x61_gremlins] reports. **Neither of those shapes appears here.** This record runs in calendar-year increments to two contractors for more than a decade, so it can answer a question the other two could not, the cost of owning an in-flight simulator.

**73 transactions across 18 awards total 29,085,924.37 dollars**, from 21 February 2014 to 30 September 2025, a span of 11.6 years \[[USAspending][ref_usaspending]\].

**Every total in this section is a reassembly and not a restatement.** The distinction earns one line of notation, because the reliability of the section rests on it.

$$
\sum_k v_k = V
\tag{2}
$$

**The registry publishes the left side and the right side independently.** The transactions are filed one at a time by the contracting office as money moves and the award total is a separate field. **Agreement between them is therefore evidence for both, and disagreement would be a defect in one.** That position is stronger than quoting either alone. **17 of the 18 agree to the cent.** The one that does not is excluded because part of it falls past this article's date \[[USAspending][ref_usaspending]\].

| Calendar year | Obligated | Share of the total |
|---|---|---|
| 2014 | 514,070.00 dollars | 1.8 percent |
| 2015 | 653,933.00 dollars | 2.2 percent |
| 2016 | 56,620.01 dollars | 0.2 percent |
| 2018 | 3,946,393.66 dollars | 13.6 percent |
| 2019 | 10,000.00 dollars | 0.0 percent |
| 2020 | 1,843,037.33 dollars | 6.3 percent |
| 2021 | 6,020,876.27 dollars | 20.7 percent |
| 2022 | 6,183,543.77 dollars | 21.3 percent |
| 2023 | 3,816,669.74 dollars | 13.1 percent |
| 2024 | 840,780.59 dollars | 2.9 percent |
| 2025 | 5,200,000.00 dollars | 17.9 percent |
| **All years** | **29,085,924.37 dollars** | **100.0 percent** |

**Two contractors hold all of it.** Calspan takes 23,611,921.77 dollars, which is 81.2 percent, and Lockheed Martin takes 5,474,002.60 dollars, which is 18.8 percent. Each share in this section, including the third column of the table above, is one subtotal divided by the whole.

$$
\rho_p = \frac{V_p}{V_{\text{all}}} , \qquad \rho_{\text{Calspan}} = \frac{23{,}611{,}921.77}{29{,}085{,}924.37} = 0.812 , \qquad \rho_{\text{Lockheed Martin}} = \frac{5{,}474{,}002.60}{29{,}085{,}924.37} = 0.188
\tag{3}
$$

**The split follows the division of labour the press releases describe**, with the laboratory responsible for the simulation system and the prime contractor for the airframe and the autonomy interface \[[VISTA X-62 Advancing Autonomy and Changing the Face of Air Power, Lockheed Martin, 13 February 2023][ref_lm_press]\].

### The Redesignation Is Visible in the Money

**Obligations run at 1,390,629.73 dollars a year before 14 June 2021 and 4,404,494.90 dollars a year after it, a ratio of 3.17** \[[USAspending][ref_usaspending]\].

**The average over the whole record is 2,506,165.10 dollars a year, and quoting that alone would conceal the finding.** A reader would compute that figure first. It is 1.76 times smaller than the rate the aeroplane has been running at since the redesignation.

**That is a comparison of averages over unequal periods and it should be read as one.** The earlier period includes two years with almost no obligations at all and one, 2018, with nearly four million. **The step is real and the smoothness is not**, and an aeroplane bought a calendar year at a time shows a lumpy record.

**The first obligation after the redesignation came 31 days later**, being 1,350,000.00 dollars for the third phase of the simulation system upgrade \[[Contract FA930421F5020, VISTA Simulation System upgrade Phase III, Department of the Air Force to Calspan][ref_usa_vss3]\]. **The redesignation and the upgrade are the same event seen from two records.**

**And the largest single obligation in the record is the most recent one.** 5,200,000.00 dollars were obligated on 30 September 2025, which equals the 2025 row of the table and is therefore 17.9 percent of everything by the share relation above, and falls 68 days before this article's date. **It is dated the last day of a fiscal year**, which this article notes without inferring anything from it.

**The record also carries 22 modifications obligating nothing and 5 deobligating a total of 68,585.40 dollars** \[[USAspending][ref_usaspending]\]. A zero-dollar modification is an administrative action against an open award and differs from spending. The previous article established that distinction and this record confirms it.

**6 transactions fall after this article's date and are excluded at the source rather than in the prose**, carrying 782,854.00 dollars between them. **One of those is the only place in the entire record where the designation X-62A appears**, so the exclusion is no formality. An article that filtered in the sentence rather than in the data would have reported the opposite of this record's most interesting property.

### The Register's Unofficial Sentence Is Corroborated by a Different Government Record

**The compiler marks the X-62A's description as not official Department of Defense wording, and the description attributes the upgrade to the Skyborg programme** \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\]. **The sentence is a reconstruction from open sources, and the compiler says so.**

**The contract record confirms it independently.** 108 days after the redesignation, the Air Force obligated 799,956.00 dollars to Lockheed Martin under a line whose description names **HAVE Autonomous Air Combat Operations Phase Two Skyborg** \[[Contract FA930421F5034, HAVE Autonomous Air Combat Operations Phase II Skyborg, Department of the Air Force to Lockheed Martin][ref_usa_haveaaco]\]. The word first appears in the 40th of the record's 73 transactions, and the record never once uses the designation.

**This deserves careful statement because the result is epistemic and not factual.** The previous article could establish that the register had stopped being a primary source and could not do anything about it. **This one can, for one sentence, because the accounting system and the designation register are independent records maintained for unrelated purposes** and they agree. **That does not make the sentence official. It makes it corroborated**, which is a weaker claim and a more useful one.

## Sizing From First Principles

**There is no airframe to size here, because the airframe is a production F-16D and The Research Question above sets it aside.** What can be sized from first principles is the instrument, being the number of independent controls a variable-stability system needs in order to reproduce another aeroplane exactly. This section takes the published list of what the second flight control system commands, derives from the model-following condition that the number required is three per axis, finds that the list supplies three per axis, and then shows that the geometry of the two lifting controls decides how well conditioned those three are.

### What the Variable Stability System Commands

**All of this article's mathematics turns on one list, and the list is published.**

In-flight simulation on this aeroplane is done by a second flight control system running in parallel with the F-16's own, engaged once the aircraft is airborne, with a safety pilot in the back seat who can take control at any moment. **That second system commands, with essentially full authority, the left and right horizontal stabilators, the ailerons, the thrust, the rudder and the trailing-edge flaps** \[[X-62A and NF-16D VISTA, GlobalSecurity.org][ref_gs_x62]\]. The surfaces it does not command are the leading-edge flaps and the speedbrakes \[[F-16 VISTA, MATV and NF-16D, Variable-stability In-flight Simulator Test Aircraft, F-16.net][ref_f16net_vista]\].

**Count them by axis, because one pair of surfaces can supply two controls.** The two stabilators, driven together and driven differentially, are two independent controls, and so are the trailing-edge surfaces, which on an F-16 are flaperons and which the second system commands both symmetrically and asymmetrically \[[F-16 VISTA, MATV and NF-16D, Variable-stability In-flight Simulator Test Aircraft, F-16.net][ref_f16net_vista]\].

**The literature on this aeroplane takes the same system as its subject.** The programmable feel system that drives the two sticks was published the year the aircraft first flew \[[Siracuse and Govindaraj 1992][ref_vista_feel_1992]\], and the simulation model built round the modified aeroplane was published twice in the following four years \[[McKeehen, Genesis Simulation of a Modified VISTA and F-16, AIAA Flight Simulation Technologies Conference, 1995][ref_vista_genesis_1995]\] \[[McKeehen et al. 1996][ref_vista_piloted_1996]\]. **The modern configuration is published in the same way**, with the simulation system, the autonomy interface and the flight testing each the subject of a separate paper \[[Haus et al. 2023][ref_scitech_vss_design]\] \[[Schiavone et al. 2023][ref_scitech_sacs]\] \[[Haus 2023][ref_scitech_vss_test]\].

**That claim deserves its one line of algebra, because it is doing real work.** The symmetric and differential commands are a change of basis on the two surface deflections, and the matrix that performs it is invertible.

$$
\begin{bmatrix} \delta_s \\ \delta_d \end{bmatrix} = \tfrac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \delta_L \\ \delta_R \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \det = - \tfrac{1}{2} \ne 0
\tag{4}
$$

**The argument needs only a non-zero determinant.** Two surfaces yield two independent commands exactly when the map between them can be undone, so the pair contributes two columns to the control effectiveness matrix. **A single all-moving tail, or two surfaces mechanically ganged, would contribute one**, and the next sections show what a missing column costs. So the system has **a symmetric stabilator, a symmetric flap and a throttle in the longitudinal axis**, and **a differential stabilator, an aileron and a rudder in the lateral-directional axis**. **3 in each.**

**An ordinary fighter, idealised in the same way, gives its pilot 1 control in pitch and 2 in roll and yaw.** The idealisation is that the stick moves one surface in pitch and that the throttle is not part of the flight control system.

**That difference is one of kind. The next section shows that it separates a problem that has an exact solution from one that does not**, and the number 3 recurs there for a reason.

### Model Following as the Mathematics of Pretending

**The programme calls what this aeroplane does the Model Following Algorithm**, and the prime contractor lists it as a deliverable alongside the simulation system and the autonomy interface \[[VISTA X-62 Advancing Autonomy and Changing the Face of Air Power, Lockheed Martin, 13 February 2023][ref_lm_press]\] \[[Caraway et al. 2023][ref_scitech_mfa]\]. **The phrase is a term of art with a definition, a solvability condition and a computable failure, and all three are older than the aeroplane.**

#### The Statement

Two linear systems are in play. The first is the host aeroplane, whose state is what the air and the metal actually do. The second is the model, which exists only inside a computer and which the host is required to imitate \[[Stevens, Lewis and Johnson, Aircraft Control and Simulation][book_stevens_lewis]\] \[[McRuer, Ashkenas and Graham, Aircraft Dynamics and Automatic Control][book_mcruer_dynamics]\].

$$
\dot{x} = A x + B u , \qquad \dot{x}_m = A_m x_m + B_m u_m
\tag{5}
$$

The simulation is achieved by a control law that watches both systems and drives the host's surfaces \[[Model reference adaptive control][ref_mrac]\].

$$
u = K_x x + K_m x_m + K_u u_m
\tag{6}
$$

Substituting one into the other gives the closed loop.

$$
\dot{x} = \left( A + B K_x \right) x + B K_m x_m + B K_u u_m
\tag{7}
$$

**For the host's state to equal the model's state at every instant, given that the two start together, the closed loop must be the model.** Matching the two expressions term by term gives a pair of conditions on the gains.

$$
B \left( K_x + K_m \right) = A_m - A , \qquad B K_u = B_m
\tag{8}
$$

**Notice what has happened. The unknowns are gains, the equations are linear in them, and the question is no longer about aeroplanes at all.** It is the question of whether two matrix equations have a solution, and that question has a standard answer.

#### The Condition Is a Subspace Containment

A linear equation of the form $ B X = Y $ has an exact solution if and only if every column of $ Y $ lies in the column space of $ B $. The projector onto the complement of that column space is built from the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse \[[Moore-Penrose inverse][ref_pseudoinverse]\] \[[Projection, the linear algebraic operation][ref_projection]\].

$$
\Pi = I - B B^{+}
\tag{9}
$$

**And the conditions for exact model following are that this projector annihilates both right-hand sides.**

$$
\Pi \left( A_m - A \right) = 0 , \qquad \Pi B_m = 0
\tag{10}
$$

**Nothing more is required. A NASA Technical Memorandum of October 1967 states and proves the result** \[[Erzberger, Analysis and Design of Model Following Control Systems by State Space Techniques, NASA Technical Memorandum X-61189, 18 October 1967][ref_erzberger_1967]\]. When the conditions hold, the gains follow immediately, and they are the least-squares solution because in this case the least-squares solution is exact \[[Asseo, Application of Optimal Control to Perfect Model Following, Journal of Aircraft, 1970][ref_asseo_1970]\].

$$
K_x + K_m = B^{+} \left( A_m - A \right) , \qquad K_u = B^{+} B_m
\tag{11}
$$

**That difference is the quantity the rest of this article is about, so it receives a name.**

$$
\Delta A = A_m - A
\tag{12}
$$

**Read the first condition in words.** The simulation demands a change of dynamics, being the difference between the model's dynamics matrix and the host's. **Every column of that difference must be producible by some combination of the host's controls.** The host's aerodynamics, its inertia, its speed and its altitude appear nowhere except through $ B $, and the model's realism appears nowhere except through $ A_m $. **The condition is about reach and not about power.**

#### What It Costs When the Condition Fails

**The instrument was built on this literature and the literature knew it.** One of Calspan's other in-flight simulators, the Total In-Flight Simulator \[[Calspan][ref_calspan]\], published its model-following system and the flight verification of it within five years of the memorandum \[[Pruner and Reynolds 1968][ref_tifs_1968]\] \[[Motyka et al. 1972][ref_tifs_1972]\]. **The mathematics and the aeroplanes that use it are the same generation**, and the X-62A is a late member of that line, long after its first. **This article does not know how many machines stand between the two**, because counting them would mean settling what makes an aeroplane a variable-stability aeroplane as distinct from merely a research one, and none of the sources read draws that line.

The literature calls the exact case **perfect model following** and the approximate case **real model following**, and it has done so since the nineteen seventies \[[Morrow and Balasubramanian 1975][ref_morrow_1975]\] \[[Lutze, A Perfect Explicit Model Following Control Solution to Imperfect Model Following Control Problems, AIAA Guidance, Navigation and Control Conference, 1989][ref_lutze_1989]\]. **Tuning does not decide the distinction. Whether a projector is zero decides it.**

When it is not zero, the least-squares gains leave a residual.

$$
E = \Pi \left( A_m - A \right)
\tag{13}
$$

And the error between the host and the model obeys an equation that repays a second reading \[[Anderson and Schmidt, Error Dynamics and Perfect Model Following With Application to Flight Control, Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics, 1991][ref_anderson_1991]\].

$$
\dot{e} = \left( A + B K_x \right) e + E x_m + \left( B K_u - B_m \right) u_m
\tag{14}
$$

**Setting the derivative to zero says how large that error settles to**, and the expression contains the residual and nothing the designer can still choose.

$$
\dot{e} = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad e_\infty = - \left( A + B K_x \right)^{-1} \Pi \, \Delta A \, x_m
\tag{15}
$$

**The first term of the error equation is a stable homogeneous response and a designer can make it as fast as the hardware allows.** The second term is not. **It is driven by the model's state**, which means that the harder the simulated aeroplane is manoeuvring, the larger the error, and no choice of $ K_x $ removes it because $ E $ does not contain $ K_x $. **A model-following error of this kind cannot be tuned away. It can only be designed away, by changing $ B $, which means by changing which surfaces the system is allowed to move.**

#### A Counting Bound States the Design in One Line

The projector's rank is fixed by the rank of the control effectiveness matrix.

$$
\operatorname{rank} \Pi = n - \operatorname{rank} B \; \ge \; n - m
\tag{16}
$$

**For the conditions to hold for an arbitrary model, the projector must be zero, and that requires the host's controls to span the whole state space.** Written out for each axis of an aeroplane, this is a counting statement about hardware.

| System | Dynamic states in the axis | Independent controls | Rank of the projector |
|---|---|---|---|
| An ordinary fighter, in pitch | 3 | 1 | 2 |
| An ordinary fighter, in roll and yaw | 3 | 2 | 1 |
| The variable stability system, in pitch | 3 | 3 | 0 |
| The variable stability system, in roll and yaw | 3 | 3 | 0 |

**The three dynamic states in the longitudinal axis are speed, angle of attack and pitch rate**, the pitch attitude being kinematic and therefore carried along by the others without needing to be commanded. The three in the lateral-directional axis are sideslip, roll rate and yaw rate, with bank angle kinematic in the same way.

**And the variable stability system has exactly three independent controls in each. That is not a coincidence and it is not generosity.** It is the smallest number that makes the projector vanish, and a system with two would face a one-dimensional subspace of demanded dynamics that no gain could produce.

**This is why the second flight control system commands the throttle.** On an ordinary fighter idealised as above a throttle is no flight control. Here it is one, because the speed equation is one of the three and no aerodynamic surface the second system commands can change the axial force independently of the normal force and the pitching moment. **The engine is not propulsion in this argument. It is the third column of a matrix.**

#### The Bound Is Sufficient and Not Necessary, and Saying So Costs Nothing

**The counting above matches every state, and a simulation does not have to.** What the pilot is given is an output rather than a state, being an attitude, a rate, a load factor and whatever the instruments show, and matching an output is a weaker demand than matching everything behind it \[[Stevens, Lewis and Johnson, Aircraft Control and Simulation][book_stevens_lewis]\].

$$
y = C x \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \left( I - \left( C B \right) \left( C B \right)^{+} \right) C \, \Delta A = 0
\tag{17}
$$

**The projector has shrunk.** It is now built from the product of the output matrix and the control matrix and no longer from the control matrix alone, and that product has at most as many rows as there are outputs. **A simulation that only has to reproduce pitch rate and normal acceleration is asking for less than one that has to reproduce the whole state vector.**

**So three controls per axis is sufficient and it is not necessary**, and this article claims only the sufficiency. **What the weaker condition buys is a warning rather than a licence.** An output-matched simulation is exact in what the pilot is shown and free to be wrong in everything else, and the states it is free to be wrong in are still driving the aeroplane. **The mismatch does not disappear. It moves somewhere the pilot is not looking.**

#### One Control Short, and Which Half of the Aeroplane Goes Wrong

**A rank deficiency of one sounds like a small defect and it is not, because the deficient direction is not distributed evenly over the aeroplane.**

Take the longitudinal short period alone, in the two states angle of attack and pitch rate, and ask a variable-stability system to turn a conventionally stable host into a statically unstable and lightly damped model. **That is the characteristic task**, because an aeroplane with dangerously poor flying qualities is what a test pilot school wants its students to meet in a machine with a safety pilot in it \[[X-62A and NF-16D VISTA, GlobalSecurity.org][ref_gs_x62]\].

The short period in those two states has a standard form, and the one below is written with the angle-of-attack equation's pitch-rate coefficient set to unity, the usual normalisation \[[Etkin and Reid, Dynamics of Flight, Stability and Control][book_etkin_reid]\] \[[Cook, Flight Dynamics Principles][book_cook]\] \[[USAF Test Pilot School, Flying Qualities Phase, Chapter 4, Equations of Motion][ref_tps_ch4]\] \[[USAF Test Pilot School, Flying Qualities Phase, Chapter 8, Dynamics][ref_tps_ch8]\].

$$
\begin{bmatrix} \dot{\alpha} \\ \dot{q} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} Z_\alpha & 1 \\ M_\alpha & M_q \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \alpha \\ q \end{bmatrix}
\tag{18}
$$

**A two-by-two matrix carries its frequency and damping in its trace and its determinant**, so a pair of matrices can be read as two aeroplanes rather than as eight numbers.

$$
\omega_n = \sqrt{\det A} , \qquad 2 \zeta \omega_n = - \operatorname{tr} A
\tag{19}
$$

**The numbers below are representative rather than measured.** The host and the model are plausible short-period pairs chosen to make the arithmetic legible, the control effectivenesses are in the ratio a horizontal tail and a trailing-edge flap stand in, and **nothing in the conclusion depends on the particular values**, only on the fact that a tail makes much more moment than lift and a flap makes much more lift than moment. The published F-16 aerodynamic data is tabular and graphical, with no closed form \[[Nguyen, Ogburn, Gilbert, Kibler, Brown and Deal, Simulator Study of Stall and Post-Stall Characteristics of a Fighter Airplane With Relaxed Longitudinal Static Stability, NASA Technical Paper 1538, December 1979][ref_tp1538]\], so the matrices below are not computed from it. The host, the model and the two pitch controls are these, with the tail as the first column of the control matrix and the trailing-edge flap as the second.

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix} -1.20 & 1.00 \\ -8.00 & -1.50 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad A_m = \begin{bmatrix} -0.60 & 1.00 \\ 2.00 & -0.40 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix} -0.09 & -0.20 \\ -9.00 & -1.00 \end{bmatrix}
\tag{20}
$$

**Read through the relation above, the two matrices describe two quite different aeroplanes.** The host has a determinant of 9.8 per second squared, which is positive, so it is an ordinary oscillatory short period at **3.13 radians per second with a damping ratio of 0.431**, giving a damped period of 2.22 seconds. **The model's determinant is -1.76, which is negative**, and a negative determinant means the pair is not oscillatory at all.

$$
\det A < 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \lambda = \tfrac{1}{2} \left( \operatorname{tr} A + \sqrt{\operatorname{tr}^2 A - 4 \det A} \right) > 0 , \qquad t_2 = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}
\tag{21}
$$

**The model diverges, with a root of 0.918 per second and a time to double amplitude of 0.755 seconds.** A negative determinant is negative longitudinal static stability, which the school's textbook gives a chapter and which the F-16 itself has below Mach 1 \[[General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon][ref_f16]\] \[[USAF Test Pilot School, Flying Qualities Phase, Chapter 5, Longitudinal Static Stability][ref_tps_ch5]\] \[[Relaxed stability][ref_relaxed_stability]\]. That is the aeroplane the student is asked to fly, and the simulation's job is to move the determinant by 11.56 per second squared, from stable to divergent, using the surfaces of an aeroplane that is neither.

With two independent pitch controls the projector has rank 0 and the residual is zero to machine precision. **With the tail alone the projector has rank 1**, and a projector onto the complement of a single column has a closed form that makes the asymmetry visible before any arithmetic is done.

$$
\Pi = I - \frac{b \, b^{\mathrm{T}}}{b^{\mathrm{T}} b}
\tag{22}
$$

**The projector removes the direction the control points in and leaves everything perpendicular to it untouched.** A tail column points almost entirely along the pitching-moment axis, so what survives the projector is almost entirely the lift axis. **The residual is therefore not spread over the problem.** Writing the surviving fraction row by row says so in numbers.

$$
\eta_\alpha = \frac{\left\| \left( \Pi \, \Delta A \right)_\alpha \right\|}{\left\| \Delta A_\alpha \right\|} , \qquad \eta_q = \frac{\left\| \left( \Pi \, \Delta A \right)_q \right\|}{\left\| \Delta A_q \right\|}
\tag{23}
$$

| Row of the dynamics matrix | Change demanded | Change unreachable | Fraction unreachable |
|---|---|---|---|
| Angle of attack | 0.6 per second | 0.5 per second | 83.3 percent |
| Pitch rate | 10.06 per second squared | 0.005 per second squared | 0.05 percent |

**With one pitch control the pitch-damping row can be retuned almost exactly and the lift row cannot be touched at all.** The ratio between the two failures is 1,677.

**The ratio is the physical content of the design, and no numerical curiosity.** A horizontal tail is a moment generator. Deflected, it changes how the aeroplane rotates and it barely changes how much lift the aeroplane makes. **So a simulator built round a tail alone can imitate any pitch stiffness and any pitch damping it likes, and it cannot imitate a different wing.**

**The quantity that stays the host's own is the one the pilot feels in the seat.**

$$
\frac{n_z}{\alpha} = \frac{\bar{q} \, S \, C_{L_\alpha}}{W}
\tag{24}
$$

**Every term on the right belongs to the host.** The dynamic pressure is the host's speed and altitude, the area is the host's wing and the slope is the host's aerodynamics. **A pitch control changes none of them**, so the acceleration a given angle of attack produces is whatever the F-16 produces, whatever the model says it should be.

**And the error a single control leaves does not decay.** For a steady one-radian angle of attack demanded of the model, the residual drives a steady angle-of-attack error of **7.6 percent** and a steady pitch-rate error of 0.409 per second. **A student flying that simulation is holding a different angle of attack from the one the model is holding, permanently, and no gain in the system removes it.**

**A symmetric trailing-edge flap is the missing column.** It makes lift with comparatively little moment, and adding it to the matrix takes the unreachable subspace from one dimension to none. **This is a reason for the variable stability system to command the trailing-edge flaps**, and the reason is visible in the arithmetic, although the designers' reasoning appears in no source consulted.

### The Determinant Is a Distance

**Two lifting controls only count as two if they act at different places, and the determinant shows it in a form that has no aerodynamics in it.**

A control surface that produces a normal force at a station aft of the centre of gravity produces a pitching moment in proportion, with the moment arm measured in mean aerodynamic chords \[[Etkin and Reid, Dynamics of Flight, Stability and Control][book_etkin_reid]\] \[[Nelson, Flight Stability and Automatic Control][book_nelson]\].

$$
M_f = - \frac{\ell_f}{\bar{c}} Z_f , \qquad M_h = - \frac{\ell_h}{\bar{c}} Z_h
\tag{25}
$$

Substituting into the two-by-two block that maps the two lifting controls onto normal force and pitching moment gives a determinant that collapses.

$$
\det \begin{bmatrix} Z_f & Z_h \\ M_f & M_h \end{bmatrix} = \frac{Z_f Z_h}{\bar{c}} \left( \ell_f - \ell_h \right)
\tag{26}
$$

**The control effectivenesses appear as a product and the geometry appears as a difference.** Make either surface twice as powerful and the determinant doubles. **Move the two surfaces to the same station and the determinant is zero however powerful they are**, because two forces applied at one point are one force.

**Independent command of lift and pitching moment is therefore a fact about where the surfaces are**, and the quantity that decides it is the separation between their centres of pressure measured in chords. For an F-16, with the flap on the wing trailing edge and the tail well aft, that separation is estimated here at about 0.6 chords, an inference from the published layout rather than a measurement.

**Conditioning is what the determinant understates.** A matrix can be invertible and still useless, because the deflections required to achieve a given change scale with the inverse of its smallest singular value \[[Condition number][ref_condition_number]\] \[[Singular value decomposition][ref_singular_value]\].

$$
\kappa = \frac{\sigma_{\max}}{\sigma_{\min}}
\tag{27}
$$

**The relation behind that sentence is displayed below, because the article has so far treated deflection as free when it is the scarcest thing the aeroplane has.** The gains solve the matching condition, the deflection is the gains acting on the state, and the worst case over states of a given size is bounded by the demanded change divided by the smallest singular value.

$$
u = \left( K_x + K_m \right) x , \qquad \left\| K_x + K_m \right\| \le \frac{\left\| \Delta A \right\|}{\sigma_{\min} \left( B \right)}
\tag{28}
$$

| Separation between the two lifting controls | Condition number |
|---|---|
| 0.6 chords, being the order of the actual layout | 7.17 |
| Half of that | 12.13 |
| Two hundredths of a chord, being effectively coincident | 157.8 |

**Halving the separation worsens the conditioning by a factor of 1.69**, and driving it to zero sends the condition number through two orders of magnitude on its way to infinity. **The deflections required to simulate a given aeroplane grow in the same proportion**, and the next section shows that deflection is the resource this aeroplane runs out of.

**The airframe fixes the separation, and no simulation software can change it.** A variable-stability aeroplane whose lifting controls happened to sit close together would be a poor instrument no matter how good its computers were, and the arithmetic says by how much.

#### The Column That Makes the Projector Vanish Is the Column That Runs Out First

**Solving the worked example for its gains rather than for its residual gives a result the rank argument does not predict.**

With two columns the control matrix is square and invertible, so the matching condition $ B \left( K_x + K_m \right) = A_m - A $ is solved by the inverse, and the angle-of-attack column of the gains comes from the angle-of-attack column of the demanded change.

$$
\Delta A = A_m - A = \begin{bmatrix} 0.60 & 0 \\ 10.00 & 1.10 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \begin{bmatrix} \gamma_s \\ \gamma_f \end{bmatrix} = B^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 0.60 \\ 10.00 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{-1.71} \begin{bmatrix} -1.00 & 0.20 \\ 9.00 & -0.09 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0.60 \\ 10.00 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -0.8187 \\ -2.6316 \end{bmatrix}
\tag{29}
$$

The simulation of the previous section therefore demands **0.82 degrees of symmetric tail and 2.63 degrees of symmetric flap for every degree of angle of attack.** Both are gradients rather than deflections, and the quotient is what matters. **The flap is asked for more than three times as much**, because it is the weaker lift producer of the two and must supply all of the change in lift.

| Surface | Demanded by a five-degree excursion | Published limit | Share of the limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Symmetric horizontal tail | 4.09 degrees | 25 degrees | 16.4 percent |
| Symmetric flap | 13.16 degrees | 21.5 degrees | 61.2 percent |

**The flap is 3.74 times closer to its stops than the tail is to its own.** Carrying the excursion up until something saturates, **the flap reaches its limit at 8.17 degrees of angle of attack and the tail would not reach its own until 30.5 degrees**. A deflection is the gradient times the excursion, a surface saturates where that product reaches its published limit, and the table and both angles follow.

$$
\delta = \left| \gamma \right| \alpha , \qquad \alpha_{\text{sat}} = \frac{\delta_{\max}}{\left| \gamma \right|} , \qquad \frac{21.5}{2.6316} = 8.17 , \qquad \frac{25}{0.8187} = 30.5 , \qquad \frac{2.6316 \times 5 / 21.5}{0.8187 \times 5 / 25} = \frac{0.6120}{0.1637} = 3.74
\tag{30}
$$

**That reverses the intuition the rank argument leaves.** The tail is the powerful surface and the flap is the afterthought, and the counting bound requires only that the flap be there. **The deflection arithmetic says the flap is what runs out**, so the envelope of aeroplanes this machine can imitate is set by its weakest control rather than by its strongest.

**The bound of the previous relation is loose here.** It gives 53.4 against a realised gain norm of 2.76, a factor of 19.4, because the worst-case direction the bound assumes is not the direction this particular simulation demands. **A bound that is loose by a factor of nineteen is a bound and not an estimate**, and the realised value is the one the table above uses.

## Dependent Systems

**The controls counted under Sizing From First Principles act through hardware the simulation did not choose, and that hardware is where the vehicle returns to the argument.** The second flight control system drives the production surfaces, and the deflection limits, rate limits and lags of the production actuators were published in 1979 \[[Nguyen, Ogburn, Gilbert, Kibler, Brown and Deal, Simulator Study of Stall and Post-Stall Characteristics of a Fighter Airplane With Relaxed Longitudinal Static Stability, NASA Technical Paper 1538, December 1979][ref_tp1538]\]. This section reads those limits as frequencies, takes the actuator lag as a floor under the delay of every simulated aeroplane, shows that the same rate limits make the instrument subject to the oscillation it is used to study, and ends with the human being and the rating scale through which every result is reported.

### The Frequency at Which the Simulation Runs Out of Authority Is Published

**NASA released the numbers that bound this aeroplane's simulation in 1979, twelve years before it flew as a simulator, in a report that never names the type in its title.**

Technical Paper 1538 studies the stall and post-stall behaviour of a fighter with relaxed longitudinal static stability, and states in its appendix on aerodynamic data that the data came from low-speed wind-tunnel tests of subscale models of the F-16 \[[Nguyen, Ogburn, Gilbert, Kibler, Brown and Deal, Simulator Study of Stall and Post-Stall Characteristics of a Fighter Airplane With Relaxed Longitudinal Static Stability, NASA Technical Paper 1538, December 1979][ref_tp1538]\]. Its Table 1 gives the mass, the inertias, the wing geometry and the surface deflection limits. **Its Appendix A gives the actuator lag and the rate limit of every surface but the speedbrake**, and those two numbers are what decide how fast a simulation can be. The speedbrake carries a deflection limit in Table 1 and no actuator anywhere, which is consistent with its not being a flight control.

#### A Rate Limit Is a Frequency in Disguise

A surface commanded to oscillate must move fastest as it passes through zero, and the peak rate is the product of the amplitude and the frequency \[[Slew rate][ref_slew_rate]\].

$$
\delta \left( t \right) = \hat{\delta} \sin \omega t \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \left| \dot{\delta} \right|_{\max} = \hat{\delta} \omega \le R
\tag{31}
$$

**Divide the rate limit by the deflection limit and the result has the dimensions of a frequency.** It is the highest frequency at which the surface can still reach its stops.

$$
\omega_c = \frac{R}{\delta_{\max}}
\tag{32}
$$

Above it the usable amplitude falls as the reciprocal of frequency, so the fraction of authority available is a simple ratio \[[Describing function][ref_describing_function]\].

$$
\frac{\hat{\delta} \left( \omega \right)}{\delta_{\max}} = \min \left( 1 , \frac{\omega_c}{\omega} \right)
\tag{33}
$$

**At the short period, for any surface whose corner frequency falls below it, that ratio alone gives the answer.**

$$
\frac{\hat{\delta} \left( \omega_{sp} \right)}{\delta_{\max}} = \frac{\omega_c}{\omega_{sp}} \qquad \text{whenever} \qquad \omega_c < \omega_{sp}
\tag{34}
$$

**These are the published limits, with the corner frequency computed from the two columns beside it.**

| Surface | Deflection limit | Rate limit | Full-deflection corner | Commanded by the second system |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Symmetric horizontal tail | 25.0 degrees | 60.0 degrees per second | 2.40 radians per second | yes |
| Differential horizontal tail, per surface | 5.375 degrees | 60.0 degrees per second | 11.16 radians per second | yes |
| Aileron, which is a flaperon on this aircraft | 21.5 degrees | 80.0 degrees per second | 3.72 radians per second | yes |
| Rudder | 30.0 degrees | 120.0 degrees per second | 4.00 radians per second | yes |
| Leading-edge flap, which the second system does not command | 25.0 degrees | 25.0 degrees per second | 1.00 radians per second | no |

**Read the fourth column and the design becomes visible.**

**The symmetric horizontal tail, which has the most deflection of any pitch surface commanded by the second system, has the lowest corner frequency of all of them at 2.4 radians per second**, or 0.382 hertz. **That is below the short-period frequency of the aeroplanes this machine exists to imitate.** A fighter short period sits in the region of 4 radians per second, a representative value this article assumes, and at that frequency the stabilator can reach only 60 percent of its travel, or 15 degrees out of twenty-five.

$$
\omega_c = \frac{60}{25} = 2.40 , \qquad \frac{\omega_c}{2 \pi} = 0.382 , \qquad \frac{\hat{\delta} \left( \omega_{sp} \right)}{\delta_{\max}} = \frac{2.40}{4} = 0.60 , \qquad \hat{\delta} = 0.60 \times 25 = 15
\tag{35}
$$

**The differential tail is the opposite case and the contrast is exact.** It has the least deflection of any of them and the same rate limit as the stabilator, so its corner frequency is higher by the ratio of the two deflection limits, 4.65 against 4.65. The common rate limit cancels.

$$
\frac{\omega_{c,d}}{\omega_{c,s}} = \frac{R / 5.375}{R / 25.0} = \frac{25.0}{5.375} = 4.65 , \qquad \frac{11.16}{2.40} = 4.65
\tag{36}
$$

**The surface with a fifth of the authority has more than four times the bandwidth at full authority**, and at the short period it is not rate limited at all.

**A designer who had sized the rate limits in proportion to the deflections would have produced the same corner frequency everywhere.** That did not happen. The rate limits run 60, 60, 80 and 120 degrees per second against deflections of 25, 5.375, 21.5 and 30, and **the four corner frequencies come out at 2.4, 11.16, 3.72 and 4 radians per second**, a spread of nearly five to one.

**This article does not know why.** The limits were set for a fighter and not for a simulator and were published twelve years before the simulator flew, and this article takes the second flight control system to have inherited them. **The inheritance is uneven, though, and the unevenness falls on the axis that matters most**, because pitch is where a variable-stability aeroplane does most of its work and the pitch surface is the slowest of the four.

#### The Leading-Edge Flap Is the Cheapest Column Nobody Bought

**The leading-edge flap has a corner frequency of exactly 1 radian per second**, being twenty-five degrees of travel at twenty-five degrees per second, and its actuator lag is 2.75 times longer than every other surface's \[[Nguyen, Ogburn, Gilbert, Kibler, Brown and Deal, Simulator Study of Stall and Post-Stall Characteristics of a Fighter Airplane With Relaxed Longitudinal Static Stability, NASA Technical Paper 1538, December 1979][ref_tp1538]\]. **It is also a direct lift device, which makes it, on paper, a fourth column for the longitudinal control matrix.**

$$
\omega_c = \frac{25.0}{25.0} = 1.00 , \qquad \frac{\tau_l}{\tau} = \frac{0.136}{0.0495} = 2.75 , \qquad \frac{\hat{\delta} \left( \omega_{sp} \right)}{\delta_{\max}} = \frac{1.00}{4} = 0.25
\tag{37}
$$

**And the second flight control system does not command it.** The published account of what the system drives lists the trailing-edge flaps and omits the leading-edge ones \[[F-16 VISTA, MATV and NF-16D, Variable-stability In-flight Simulator Test Aircraft, F-16.net][ref_f16net_vista]\].

**The arithmetic above is a sufficient reason and this article offers it as a reading rather than as a finding.** A surface that can reach only 25 percent of its travel at the short-period frequency, through an actuator 2.75 times slower than the others, adds a column to the matrix that is almost empty in the band where the simulation lives.

**The third reason is that the surface is already spoken for, and the schedule that speaks for it is published in the same appendix as the actuator lag.**

$$
\delta_l = 1.38 \, \frac{2 s + \omega_p}{s + \omega_p} \, \alpha - 9.05 \, \frac{\bar{q}}{P_s} + 1.45 , \qquad \omega_p = 7.25
\tag{38}
$$

**Read the three terms.** A lead network on angle of attack, a subtraction proportional to the ratio of dynamic to static pressure, and a constant bias. The network passes 1.38 degrees of flap per degree of angle of attack in steady flight and asks for 2.76 above its pole, because its numerator's coefficient of the Laplace variable is twice its denominator's. **It is a lead of two, with a zero at 3.625 and a pole at 7.25 radians per second.**

**And the actuator that has to execute it has a corner of 7.35 radians per second**, which is 1.42 percent from the schedule's pole. Putting the two in series shows what the surface does.

$$
\frac{\delta_l \left( s \right)}{\alpha \left( s \right)} = 1.38 \, \frac{2 s + \omega_p}{s + \omega_p} \cdot \frac{1}{\tau_l s + 1} , \qquad \omega_p \tau_l = 0.986
\tag{39}
$$

**The product of the schedule's pole and the actuator's time constant is 0.986.** If the two corners coincided exactly it would be one. **They very nearly do**, so the pole the network introduces and the pole the hardware introduces sit on top of one another, and above that frequency the combined response has one zero and two poles and therefore falls rather than rises.

| Quantity | Between one and fifteen radians per second |
|---|---|
| Gain rise the schedule commands | 1.8 |
| Gain rise the surface delivers | 0.8 |
| Shortfall | 2.25 |

**The schedule asks the flap to become nearly twice as active across that band and the flap becomes slightly less active**, and by fifteen radians per second the combined response lags by 51.7 degrees. **The lead is not merely reduced. Its sign is reversed.**

The table and the phase both come from the series transfer function above, evaluated on the imaginary axis. The gain rises are ratios of its magnitude at fifteen and at one radian per second, with and without the actuator factor.

$$
\left| \frac{\delta_l}{\alpha} \left( j \omega \right) \right| = 1.38 \, \frac{\sqrt{4 \omega^2 + \omega_p^2}}{\sqrt{\omega^2 + \omega_p^2}} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau_l^2 \omega^2 + 1}} , \qquad \varphi \left( \omega \right) = \arctan \frac{2 \omega}{\omega_p} - \arctan \frac{\omega}{\omega_p} - \arctan \tau_l \omega
\tag{40}
$$

$$
\frac{1.853}{1.028} = 1.80 , \qquad \frac{1.853 \times 0.440}{1.028 \times 0.991} = 0.80 , \qquad \frac{1.80}{0.80} = 2.25 , \qquad \varphi \left( 15 \right) = 76.4 - 64.2 - 63.9 = - 51.7 \ \text{degrees}
\tag{41}
$$

**This article makes no claim that the coincidence was deliberate or that anyone has noticed it.** The schedule was designed for an aeroplane and the actuator was sized for a surface, and a near-cancellation between two poles chosen for different purposes is as likely to be an accident as a design. **The surface the simulation might have wanted is in any case already carrying a command it cannot execute**, a third reason on top of the two the previous paragraphs give, and the public record does not say which of the three governed.

### The Actuator Puts a Floor Under Every Aeroplane This One Can Be

**The most important consequence of the published numbers is not a limit on authority. It is a limit on quickness, and it is one-sided.**

Every surface but the leading-edge flap is modelled as a first-order lag of 0.0495 seconds \[[Nguyen, Ogburn, Gilbert, Kibler, Brown and Deal, Simulator Study of Stall and Post-Stall Characteristics of a Fighter Airplane With Relaxed Longitudinal Static Stability, NASA Technical Paper 1538, December 1979][ref_tp1538]\].

$$
\frac{\delta \left( s \right)}{\delta_c \left( s \right)} = \frac{1}{\tau s + 1} , \qquad \omega_a = \frac{1}{\tau}
\tag{42}
$$

That corner frequency is 20.2 radians per second, or 3.22 hertz, and the phase it costs grows with frequency.

$$
\varphi \left( \omega \right) = - \arctan \left( \omega \tau \right)
\tag{43}
$$

**At the short period it is 11.2 degrees**, and at low frequency the lag behaves as a pure time delay of the same time constant.

$$
\frac{1}{\tau s + 1} \; \simeq \; e^{- \tau s} \qquad \text{whenever} \qquad \omega \tau \ll 1
\tag{44}
$$

**The approximation is very good across the band this article uses.** The phase a first-order lag contributes differs from a pure delay's by 0.018 of a degree at two radians per second, 0.145 at four and 1.086 at eight. **So calling the actuator a delay of 49.5 milliseconds describes the hardware and is no mere convenience.**

**Now consider what a model-following system is.** It reads a command, computes what the model would do, and moves the host's surfaces to make the host do it. **Every delay in the host therefore sits between the pilot's hand and the simulated response**, and equivalent delays in series add.

$$
\tau_e \left( \text{host and model} \right) = \tau_e \left( \text{host} \right) + \tau_e \left( \text{model} \right) \; \ge \; \tau_e \left( \text{host} \right)
\tag{45}
$$

**That inequality carries the argument, and it has no escape in it.** Both terms are non-negative, so the sum is at least the first, and the first comes from the host's actuators.

$$
\tau_s \; \ge \; \tau + \frac{3}{2 f_s}
\tag{46}
$$

**A variable-stability aeroplane can make any aeroplane sluggish and it cannot make any aeroplane crisp.** It can add lag, it can add instability, it can add a hundred milliseconds of transport delay and show a student what that feels like. **It cannot subtract its own hardware.** The set of aeroplanes it can faithfully reproduce is bounded below, and the bound is the host's equivalent delay.

**The floor is at least 49.5 milliseconds from the actuator alone.** A digital implementation adds sampling and transport. **Assuming a frame rate of sixty hertz**, which this article assumes and does not know, the computation contributes half a frame of sampling and one frame of transport, a further 16.7 and 16.7 halved, **for a floor of about 74.5 milliseconds and 17.1 degrees of phase at the short period**.

**The frame rate is an assumption and the article flags it as one.** The actuator number is published and the conclusion does not depend on the assumed part, because a floor of forty-nine and a half milliseconds is already a floor. **The assumption yields an order of magnitude for the computational share, and that share is comparable to the hardware rather than negligible beside it.**

### The Instrument Shares the Failure Mode of the Thing It Studies

**A rate-limited actuator is a recognised mechanism of pilot-induced oscillation, and this aeroplane's actuators are rate limited** \[[Pilot-induced oscillation][ref_pio]\].

Pilot-induced oscillation, for which aircraft-pilot coupling has been proposed as a replacement term because the oscillation is not necessarily the pilot's fault, is a sustained or unstable oscillation of the closed loop formed by a human operator and an aircraft \[[Pilot-induced oscillation][ref_pio]\] \[[McRuer and Krendel, Mathematical Models of Human Pilot Behavior][book_mcruer_pilot]\]. **The linear case is understood and designed against.** A category that has proved hard to predict, and to which the 1992 crash of the YF-22 prototype was linked, is the one in which the aircraft is linear until a surface hits its rate limit, at which point the effective phase lag jumps and a loop that was stable a moment earlier is not \[[Pilot-induced oscillation][ref_pio]\].

**The mechanism is the describing function of the rate limiter**, the effective gain a nonlinear element presents to a sinusoid of a given amplitude and frequency \[[Describing function][ref_describing_function]\] \[[Slotine and Li, Applied Nonlinear Control][book_slotine]\].

**A rate limiter deep in saturation is moving at its limit throughout the cycle**, so its output is not a distorted sinusoid but a triangle, and the triangle's amplitude follows from the limit and the frequency alone.

$$
\left| \dot{\delta} \right| = R \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \hat{\delta}_o = \frac{\pi R}{2 \omega}
\tag{47}
$$

The fundamental of a triangular wave is eight over pi squared times its amplitude, so the gain the element presents is the quotient of that fundamental and the input.

$$
\left| N \right| = \frac{8}{\pi^2} \cdot \frac{\hat{\delta}_o}{\hat{\delta}} = \frac{4 R}{\pi \, \hat{\delta} \, \omega}
\tag{48}
$$

**The gain falls as the reciprocal of frequency and as the reciprocal of amplitude**, an amplitude-dependent bandwidth that makes the phenomenon hard to predict from a linear model. **The tighter the pilot tries to control, the larger the command and the smaller the gain the aeroplane returns.** The result is a positive feedback between effort and difficulty, and it explains why the phenomenon appears in demanding tasks and is absent in gentle ones.

| Condition | Onset ratio | Triangular output | Gain | Amplitude lost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Full tail travel at the short period | 0.6 | 23.56 degrees | 0.764 | 23.6 percent |
| Full tail travel at ten radians per second | 0.24 | 9.42 degrees | 0.306 | 69.4 percent |

**The relation above is the deep-saturation asymptote and not the describing function itself, and the clearest evidence for that is that it exceeds one at onset.** Evaluated where the demanded rate exactly equals the limit it gives 1.273, and a rate limiter cannot amplify. **The true describing function is continuous and equals one there**, so the figures in the first row of that table, taken near onset, are indicative rather than exact, while the second row is well inside the asymptote's range.

**And the phase is the part this article cannot supply.** An ideal rate limiter, one that simply clips the slope of its input, is an even operation on an odd input and contributes no phase lag at all. **The phase lag that makes this phenomenon dangerous comes from the servo loop wrapped around the limiter in any real actuator**, and its size depends on the loop gain and the loop's dynamics. **This article has the actuator's lag and its rate limit and does not have its loop**, so it reports the gain loss and declines to quote a phase.

**The phenomenon has been flown deliberately and reported.** A limited flight test investigation of pilot-induced oscillation due to elevator rate limiting exists in the defence registry. That investigation is this section's argument flown in an aeroplane \[[Kish et al. 1997a][ref_pio_rate_limit_1997]\].

**A variable-stability aeroplane exists in part to study this**, because putting a student in a machine that can be made to oscillate under a safety pilot's supervision is safer than discovering the property on a prototype. The school that operates this aircraft says so directly, describing its purpose as giving students the opportunity to practise testing aircraft with dangerously poor flying qualities \[[X-62A and NF-16D VISTA, GlobalSecurity.org][ref_gs_x62]\].

**And the instrument contains the nonlinearity it is used to investigate.** The second flight control system drives the same surfaces, on this article's assumption through the same actuators with the same published rate limits. **When the simulated aeroplane demands a stabilator motion beyond 2.4 radians per second at full travel, the full-deflection corner of the limits table, the host rate limits**, and the phase that costs is added to the simulated response. **The student meets a lag that belongs to the host rather than to the model, and nothing in the cockpit distinguishes the two.**

**No criticism of the aeroplane is intended. The point describes what an in-flight simulator is.** Every simulator has an unmodelled remainder, and a reason a flying one is preferred to a ground-based one is that its remainder is an aeroplane rather than a motion platform. **The remainder is still there.** Stated carefully, the machine simulates the model plus itself, the sum is what the pilot rates, and separating the two is a question about the instrument rather than about the aeroplane under study.

**The published limits say where the separation matters.** Below 2.4 radians per second at full stabilator travel, and proportionately higher at smaller amplitudes, the host's rate limits are not active and the simulation is whatever the linear analysis predicts. **Above them the host is contributing a nonlinearity of its own**, and a result obtained there is a result about a particular F-16 with a particular set of hydraulic actuators.

#### What the Delay Floor Costs the Pilot

**Manual control theory's central result is that a trained operator adapts until the open loop looks like an integrator near the frequency at which the loop gain passes unity** \[[McRuer and Krendel, Mathematical Models of Human Pilot Behavior][book_mcruer_pilot]\] \[[McRuer, Ashkenas and Graham, Aircraft Dynamics and Automatic Control][book_mcruer_dynamics]\].

$$
Y_p \left( s \right) Y_c \left( s \right) \; \simeq \; \frac{\omega_{co} \, e^{- \tau_e s}}{s}
\tag{49}
$$

**The consequence is that the pilot supplies whatever the aeroplane lacks, and the one thing no adaptation supplies is phase.** An integrator alone leaves ninety degrees of margin at crossover, and a transport delay eats into it linearly.

$$
\varphi_m = \frac{\pi}{2} - \omega_{co} \tau_e
\tag{50}
$$

**So the delay floor is a fixed tax on the pilot's margin, charged before the simulated aeroplane has contributed anything.**

| At a crossover of | The actuator alone costs | The floor costs | Leaving |
|---|---|---|---|
| Three radians per second | 8.51 degrees | 12.81 degrees | 77.19 degrees |
| Six radians per second | 17.02 degrees | 25.61 degrees | 64.39 degrees |

**At the lower of the two crossover frequencies assumed here, the host consumes 14.23 percent of the available margin. At the upper it consumes 28.46 percent.** The share is the phase the floor costs divided by the ninety degrees an integrator leaves, with the floor of 74.5 milliseconds.

$$
\frac{\omega_{co} \tau_e}{\pi / 2} , \qquad \frac{3 \times 0.0745}{1.5708} = 0.1423 , \qquad \frac{6 \times 0.0745}{1.5708} = 0.2846
\tag{51}
$$

The crossover frequencies are assumed and are named as assumptions. **The delay is published.**

**Setting the margin to zero gives the frequency at which the host's hardware forbids a loop closure outright.**

$$
\varphi_m = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \omega_{co} = \frac{\pi}{2 \tau_e}
\tag{52}
$$

**That is 21.08 radians per second for the floor and 31.73 for the actuator alone.** Both are far above where a human pilot works, **so the ceiling is not the binding constraint.** What binds is the tax, which is paid at every crossover frequency and which the simulation cannot refund.

#### Why the Bandwidth Criterion Is Not Used

**The field has a standard way of turning a delay into a handling-qualities level and this article does not use it.**

The bandwidth criterion pairs a frequency at which the pitch attitude response has fallen to a stated phase with a second parameter called the phase delay, and draws a boundary in the plane of the two \[[Hodgkinson, Aircraft Handling Qualities][book_hodgkinson]\] \[[USAF Test Pilot School, Flying Qualities Phase, Volume II, Chapter 15, Dynamic Parameter Analysis][ref_tps_ch15]\]. **The delay floor derived under The Actuator Puts a Floor Under Every Aeroplane This One Can Be ought to be expressed in that parameter**, because a pure delay is the simplest thing that has one.

**And the definition is a formula that cannot be verified without reading the specification, which lies outside what this article read.** Deriving the phase delay of a pure delay from an unverified statement of the definition, not taken from the specification, gives half the delay. **The gloss the subject is usually summarised with holds that the phase delay of a pure delay is the delay.** Those two cannot both be right, and the disagreement is a factor of two on the one quantity the criterion would have supplied.

**An unverified formula is not a citation, and a factor of two is not a rounding.** So the article uses the phase margin instead, which follows from the crossover model in one line and which is derived above, and it records here that the criterion exists and that this is why it is absent. **The specification that defines it is cited and is not quoted** \[[Chalk et al. 1969][ref_8785b_background]\].

**The cost of that refusal is stated rather than hidden.** A reader who wants the delay floor expressed as a handling-qualities level will not find it here. **What is here instead is the phase it consumes at a stated crossover**, which is a weaker claim, which is derived, and which does not depend on a document this article has not opened.

### The Answer Comes Back on an Ordinal Scale

**Whatever this aeroplane measures, it reports through a human being, and the reporting scale has a property that bounds what can be done with the answer.**

The standard instrument is the Cooper-Harper rating scale, which is a decision tree ending in ten numbered boxes \[[Cooper and Harper, The Use of Pilot Rating in the Evaluation of Aircraft Handling Qualities, NASA Technical Note D-5153, 1969][ref_cooper_harper_1969]\] \[[Cooper-Harper rating scale][ref_cooper_harper]\] \[[Hodgkinson, Aircraft Handling Qualities][book_hodgkinson]\]. A pilot answers a sequence of questions about whether the aircraft is controllable, whether adequate performance is attainable, and what compensation is required, and arrives at a number between one and ten. **The numbers are ordered and the ordering is meaningful.** A rating of three describes an aeroplane better than a rating of five.

**The school that flies this aeroplane teaches that paper as a numbered chapter of its own textbook.** The United States Air Force Test Pilot School publishes its Flying Qualities Phase volume chapter by chapter into the defence registry, and **Chapter 16 is a reprint of NASA Technical Note D-5153** \[[USAF Test Pilot School, Flying Qualities Phase, Chapter 16, Reprint of NASA Technical Note D-5153][ref_tps_ch16]\]. The chapters on either side of it are the ordinary apparatus of the subject, being an introduction, the equations of motion, longitudinal static stability, dynamics, high angle of attack, flight control systems and dynamic parameter analysis \[[USAF Test Pilot School, Flying Qualities, Chapter 1, Introduction to Flying Qualities][ref_tps_ch1]\] \[[USAF Test Pilot School, Flying Qualities Phase, Chapter 4, Equations of Motion][ref_tps_ch4]\] \[[USAF Test Pilot School, Flying Qualities Phase, Chapter 5, Longitudinal Static Stability][ref_tps_ch5]\] \[[USAF Test Pilot School, Flying Qualities Phase, Chapter 8, Dynamics][ref_tps_ch8]\] \[[USAF Test Pilot School, Flying Qualities Flight Testing Phase, Chapter 10, High Angle of Attack][ref_tps_ch10]\] \[[USAF Test Pilot School, Flying Qualities Phase, Chapter 14, Flight Control Systems][ref_tps_ch14]\] \[[USAF Test Pilot School, Flying Qualities Phase, Volume II, Chapter 15, Dynamic Parameter Analysis][ref_tps_ch15]\].

**So the loop between the instrument and its readout is closed inside one institution and it is documented.** The aeroplane produces the stimulus, the student produces the rating, and the definition of the rating is bound into the curriculum the student was taught from. **That is a strength and a limit at the same time**, because a scale taught as a chapter is a scale applied consistently, and consistency is not the same thing as an interval.

**The spacing is not meaningful, and that is a property of the scale rather than an opinion about it** \[[Level of measurement][ref_ordinal]\].
