There is no sense in which the distance from three to five equals the distance from six to eight. The boundaries between the three handling-qualities levels fall between ratings three and four and between six and seven \[[Hoh 1982][research_hoh_1982]\], and those two boundaries are the scale's only claims about magnitude. **Those levels are the specification's vocabulary**, and the reasoning behind them is written down in the background documents that accompany the flying-qualities specifications rather than in the specifications themselves \[[Chalk et al. 1969][ref_8785b_background]\] \[[Crombie and Moorhouse 1980][ref_affdl_symposium_1980]\]. **The other seven gaps assert nothing.**

**The formal statement is about which transformations of the scale leave it saying the same thing.** An ordinal scale is one whose content survives any strictly increasing relabelling of its points.

$$
r_1 < r_2 \; \iff \; g \left( r_1 \right) < g \left( r_2 \right) \qquad \text{for every strictly increasing } g
\tag{53}
$$

**So a statistic is meaningful on such a scale exactly when it commutes with every such relabelling**, and that single test separates the summaries that are allowed from the summaries that are not.

$$
\operatorname{med} \left( g \left( r \right) \right) = g \left( \operatorname{med} \left( r \right) \right) , \qquad \operatorname{mean} \left( g \left( r \right) \right) \ne g \left( \operatorname{mean} \left( r \right) \right)
\tag{54}
$$

**The median is the middle element and relabelling the elements does not change which one is in the middle.** The mean is a sum divided by a count, and a sum depends on the distances between the labels, and those distances are what an ordinal scale declines to supply.

**The consequence is that a mean pilot rating is a category error.** So is a standard deviation of pilot ratings, and so is any statistical procedure that assumes the intervals are equal. **The defensible summaries are the median, the range and the counts in each level**, and the defensible tests are rank-based ones.

**Whether the practice of averaging is common is not something this article is in a position to say**, because that would require reading a sample of the handling-qualities literature large enough to support the claim and this survey has not done it. **What can be said is that the scale's definition forbids it**, that the alternative is not difficult, and that an instrument whose output is ordinal cannot be made interval by the precision of the aeroplane feeding it.

**This is the one limit in the article that is not a limit on the aeroplane at all.** The model-following condition is exact, the residual is computable, the rate limits are published, the delay floor is arithmetic. **And the quantity all of that machinery exists to deliver is a number a human being picks out of ten boxes.** The instrument is far more precise than its readout. That is an unusual place for an engineering system to be, and it deserves plain statement.

## The Flight Test Record

**The aeroplane has a flight record of more than thirty years and this article holds almost none of its data.** It first flew in April 1992 \[[General Dynamics X-62 VISTA][ref_x62_wikipedia]\] \[[Flight Test Files, Viper X, Vintage Aviation News][ref_vintage_viper_x]\]. Behind its General Electric engine with an axisymmetric vectoring exhaust nozzle it completed 95 test flights of thrust-vectoring work before that programme ended in 1994 \[[X-62 Variable-Stability In-Flight Test Aircraft, Air and Space Forces Magazine weapons and platforms entry][ref_afa_x62]\]. A Pratt and Whitney vectoring programme was planned next and was cancelled, and the aeroplane returned to its operators with a standard F100-PW-229 in June 1997 \[[F-16 VISTA, MATV and NF-16D, Variable-stability In-flight Simulator Test Aircraft, F-16.net][ref_f16net_vista]\]. The school that operates it describes its purpose as giving students the opportunity to practise testing aircraft with dangerously poor flying qualities, with a safety pilot in the back seat \[[X-62A and NF-16D VISTA, GlobalSecurity.org][ref_gs_x62]\].

**The flights since the redesignation are documented as claims and not as data.** The subsection The Autonomy the Number Was For reports the seventeen hours of flight under an artificial intelligence agent in December 2022, the twenty-one flights the trade press counts and the engagements against crewed fighters in 2023, and it reports all of them as claims by interested parties. The programme's own papers on ground and flight testing the simulation system and on flight testing the autonomy exist \[[Haus 2023][ref_scitech_vss_test]\] \[[Cotting et al. 2023c][ref_scitech_flight_testing]\], and The Source Base records that this article cites them for their existence, their authorship and their subject without having read them. **No sortie log, flight count beyond those quoted or measured response from any campaign is reported here**, and the record this article holds is silent on what those flights measured.

### The Autonomy the Number Was For

**The programme the redesignation served has a stated challenge problem and it is not flying.** The agency describes its Air Combat Evolution effort, abbreviated ACE, as seeking to increase trust in combat autonomy by using human-machine collaborative dogfighting as its challenge problem, and says that in parallel it will implement methods to measure, calibrate, increase and predict human trust in that autonomy \[[ACE, Air Combat Evolution, Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency programme page][ref_darpa_ace]\].

**Trust is the deliverable and the dogfight is the test case.** That ordering is unusual. The stated aim is a hierarchical division in which a human keeps the high-level decisions, being the engagement strategy, the choice and priority of targets and the weapon or effect, while the machine keeps the details of manoeuvre and tactics \[[ACE, Air Combat Evolution, Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency programme page][ref_darpa_ace]\]. **The pilot is to become a mission commander, and the aeroplane's role is to make that division credible enough to be trusted.**

**The aircraft was flown by an artificial intelligence agent for more than seventeen hours in December 2022**, which the prime contractor described at the time as the first occasion on which such an agent had been engaged on a tactical aircraft \[[VISTA X-62 Advancing Autonomy and Changing the Face of Air Power, Lockheed Martin, 13 February 2023][ref_lm_press]\]. The trade press records the same campaign as twenty-one flights and describes the aircraft as the first supersonic aeroplane to fly under such control, progressing to engagements against crewed fighters in 2023 \[[X-62 Variable-Stability In-Flight Test Aircraft, Air and Space Forces Magazine weapons and platforms entry][ref_afa_x62]\].

**All of these are claims by interested parties and this article reports them as such.** The agency, the prime contractor and the school all have reasons to describe the result as a first. **Nothing in this survey's 7,000 records contradicts any of them**, which describes what was searched rather than what is true.

#### The Autonomy Fits the Same Three Controls

**What makes this aeroplane useful for autonomy work is the property established under Model Following as the Mathematics of Pretending**, and it is not obvious from the press releases.

An autonomous agent developed for an uncrewed aircraft is written against that aircraft's dynamics. **To fly it on a host, the host must present the agent with the dynamics it expects**, which is model following with the model supplied by whichever vehicle the agent was built for. **The upgrade programme added a system for autonomous control of the simulation alongside an updated simulation system**, together with the model-following algorithm itself \[[VISTA X-62 Advancing Autonomy and Changing the Face of Air Power, Lockheed Martin, 13 February 2023][ref_lm_press]\] \[[Cotting et al. 2023b][ref_scitech_capabilities]\] \[[Cotting et al. 2023c][ref_scitech_flight_testing]\].

**So the agent commands a simulated aeroplane, the simulation runs on a real one, and a safety pilot sits behind both.** The projector being zero is what makes the middle layer honest, and the statement it licenses is an equality between transfer functions rather than a resemblance.

$$
\Pi = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad G_{cl} \left( s \right) = C \left( s I - A_m \right)^{-1} B_m = G_m \left( s \right)
\tag{55}
$$

**When the projector vanishes, the thing the agent is flying is not an approximation of the model. It is the model.** The host's dynamics matrix has been cancelled out of the closed loop entirely and what remains contains only the model's. **If the host could not reproduce the target vehicle's dynamics exactly, the agent would be flying something other than the aeroplane it was trained on**, and a result obtained that way would say less than it appeared to.

**And that equality holds only inside the band the previous sections bounded.** It assumes the actuators keep up, which the rate limits deny above a few radians per second at large amplitude, and it assumes no delay, which the floor denies at every frequency. **The equivalence is exact in the algebra and approximate in the aeroplane**, and the size of the approximation is what this article has spent its arithmetic measuring.

**This is the clearest answer the article has to why the aeroplane received an X number in 2021 and not in 1992.** The machine did not change. **The thing being deceived did.** For twenty-nine years it fooled pilots, a task with a well-developed literature and a well-understood instrument. **Since 2021 it has been fooling software**, and the question of whether a piece of software can tell that it is not flying the aeroplane it thinks it is flying is barely a literature yet. Among this survey's titles, one evaluates the autonomous flying qualities of a simulated variable-stability aircraft \[[Hamidani and Kunz 2018][research_hamidani_kunz_2018]\] and one quantifies the gap between simulation and reality for autonomous ground systems \[[Waheed et al. 2025][research_waheed_areti_2025]\].

## Comparison With Ground Prediction

**Every number this article computes is a ground prediction, and none of them has a flight value beside it.** The Flight Test Record, above, establishes that this article holds no measured response from any of the aeroplane's flights, so the comparison this section exists to make can be set up and cannot be completed.

**The published limits are themselves ground data.** The deflection limits, rate limits and actuator lags come from Technical Paper 1538, whose aerodynamic data came from low-speed wind-tunnel tests of subscale models of the F-16 \[[Nguyen, Ogburn, Gilbert, Kibler, Brown and Deal, Simulator Study of Stall and Post-Stall Characteristics of a Fighter Airplane With Relaxed Longitudinal Static Stability, NASA Technical Paper 1538, December 1979][ref_tp1538]\], and they describe a production F-16 as modelled in 1979. Epistemic State, below, records that the sources consulted give no current values for this aeroplane, so even the inputs to the predictions are untested against the airframe that flies.

**This article makes four predictions.** Sizing From First Principles predicts that three independent controls per axis suffice for exact model following, and that in a representative short-period simulation the symmetric flap reaches its limit at a far lower angle of attack than the tail. Dependent Systems predicts that the symmetric tail is rate limited above 2.4 radians per second at full travel, and that the host adds a published floor of actuator delay to every aeroplane it simulates. **None of the four was compared with flight**, and the flap figure uses representative matrices rather than the aeroplane's own.

**The programme made ground predictions of its own and published them, and whatever comparison they contain lies in papers outside this article's reading.** Piloted ground simulation of the modified aeroplane was published in 1995 and 1996 \[[McKeehen, Genesis Simulation of a Modified VISTA and F-16, AIAA Flight Simulation Technologies Conference, 1995][ref_vista_genesis_1995]\] \[[McKeehen et al. 1996][ref_vista_piloted_1996]\], and a paper on ground and flight testing the new simulation system was published in 2023 \[[Haus 2023][ref_scitech_vss_test]\]. What those papers set side by side is not represented here.

**The nearest comparison the article does report is on a different aeroplane.** The model-following system of Calspan's Total In-Flight Simulator was published together with its flight verification within five years of the 1967 memorandum \[[Motyka et al. 1972][ref_tifs_1972]\]. That places the mathematics this article uses inside a tradition that tested it in the air. It does not test any figure computed here for the X-62A.

**The autonomy flights carry an implied comparison and the record states only its outcome.** An agent written against one vehicle's dynamics is a product of the ground, and flying it on the host tests whether the host presents the dynamics the agent expects. The sources report that the agent flew the aeroplane for more than seventeen hours in December 2022 \[[VISTA X-62 Advancing Autonomy and Changing the Face of Air Power, Lockheed Martin, 13 February 2023][ref_lm_press]\], and nothing this article has read reports how closely the flown response matched the model.

## What the Data Changed

**This article can report no finding that the aeroplane's flight data changed, because it holds none of that data.** What it can report is what changed around the aeroplane, and each change is documented in a record other than a flight log.

**The designation changed, and its operator tied the change to the research.** The school said at the time that the redesignation reflected the research done on the aircraft over nearly thirty years \[[X-62A and NF-16D VISTA, GlobalSecurity.org][ref_gs_x62]\]. No other statement in the record connects the number to what the aeroplane had measured, and it concerns an accumulation of research rather than any single result.

**The money changed.** Obligations ran at about three times their earlier annual rate after 14 June 2021, as What It Costs to Keep an Instrument Flying states, and the first obligation after the redesignation paid for the third phase of the simulation system upgrade \[[Contract FA930421F5020, VISTA Simulation System upgrade Phase III, Department of the Air Force to Calspan][ref_usa_vss3]\].

**The subject changed.** The Flight Test Record carries the argument that since 2021 the thing being deceived has been software rather than pilots, and the prime contractor's expansion of the acronym now names the simulation as the variable quantity in place of the stability \[[VISTA X-62 Advancing Autonomy and Changing the Face of Air Power, Lockheed Martin, 13 February 2023][ref_lm_press]\]. **The record this article holds does not settle whether either change was driven by what earlier flights had shown.**

The survey behind this article holds **7,000 records**, and The Source Base, below, states the rule that admits them. **979 of them, 14.0 percent, are report primaries**, by the identifier rule set out under The Definition of Primary. 6,614 records carry a usable year, running from 1927 to 2027 with a median of 2004. **5,680 of those, 85.9 percent, predate or share the year in which the aeroplane was redesignated.**

**Every record the survey holds is cited below, each under exactly one cluster.** The clusters are ordered from the keystone outward, and a record is filed under the cluster its title names as its subject.

### Model following, which is the mathematics of pretending

**The keystone.** Explicit, implicit and perfect model following, model-reference adaptive control, dynamic inversion as a way of imposing a model, and control allocation, which distributes a demanded change over redundant surfaces. Model-reference control of plants other than aircraft is kept, because the method is the subject.

### The characteristic failure, being pilot-induced oscillation and rate limiting

**The failure the instrument shares.** Pilot-induced oscillation and aircraft-pilot coupling, actuator rate and position saturation and the anti-windup methods that treat it, and the describing functions and limit-cycle analysis that predict it.

### Designing the loop

**The design discipline around the keystone.** Flight control law design, among it fly-by-wire and digital flight control, eigenstructure assignment, quantitative feedback theory, the structured singular value, gain scheduling, reconfigurable and fault-tolerant control, and flight envelope protection.

**The airframe's earlier work and its neighbours.** High angle of attack aerodynamics, post-stall flight, departure and spin, forebody vortex control and thrust vectoring, including the programmes that flew the same subject on other aeroplanes.
