## Where the Framing Breaks Down

**The framing of this article is that the vehicle drops out of the argument, and it does not drop out entirely.** The Research Question sets the airframe aside on the ground that the condition for exact model following is about the host's controls and not about its performance. That holds for the algebra. It fails in four places, and the article says so at each of them.

**The hardware returns through the actuators.** The rate limits and the actuator lag belong to the host, so the instrument simulates the model plus itself, and the equivalence a vanishing projector licenses holds exactly only in the algebra. Dependent Systems measures by how much, and the account of the autonomy flights states the same limit for that work.

**The numbers are not the aeroplane's.** The worked residual and the deflection figures use representative short-period matrices, because the published F-16 aerodynamic data is tabular and graphical \[[Nguyen, Ogburn, Gilbert, Kibler, Brown and Deal, Simulator Study of Stall and Post-Stall Characteristics of a Fighter Airplane With Relaxed Longitudinal Static Stability, NASA Technical Paper 1538, December 1979][ref_tp1538]\], and the rate limits are those of a production F-16 as modelled in 1979. What survives is a statement about the shape of the problem, which Epistemic State distinguishes from a measurement of this aeroplane.

**The count stands on a list the article has not seen in a primary source.** Three controls per axis depends on a six-item list of commanded surfaces taken from two secondary web references \[[X-62A and NF-16D VISTA, GlobalSecurity.org][ref_gs_x62]\] \[[F-16 VISTA, MATV and NF-16D, Variable-stability In-flight Simulator Test Aircraft, F-16.net][ref_f16net_vista]\], and a single wrong entry would take a column from its axis and stop the projector vanishing.

**The readout is less precise than the instrument.** Dependent Systems closes with the Cooper-Harper scale, which is ordinal, so however exact the simulation, the result returns as a number a human being picks out of ten boxes. **The framing can measure the instrument and cannot measure the judgement the instrument exists to inform.**

## The Source Base

**The survey's 7,000 research records come from the Crossref registry, the NASA technical reports server and the Defense Technical Information Center, and every one of them is cited in the section headed The Contemporary Literature.** A further 155 definitions are hand-written, being 79 primary documents and encyclopaedic anchors, 14 books and 62 back-references to earlier articles in this series.

### The Definition of Primary

**A report primary here means an item served by the NASA technical reports server or registered under the Defense Technical Information Center's prefix, 10.21236.** The survey holds 979 of them, 14.0 percent of 7,000 records. **A further 14 report primaries are among the 155 hand-written definitions**, and they are counted separately because the survey statistic describes the survey's research records. **Folding a curated citation into a survey ratio would make the ratio mean two things at once.** The rule reaches the report literature and the school's textbook chapters and does not reach the journal and conference papers in which most of the model-following and loop-design work is published, so 14.0 percent is a lower bound on how much of the survey is first-hand.

### Where the Report Primaries Are, and Where They Are Not

**The report primaries are not spread evenly over the clusters.**

| Cluster | Records | Report primaries | Share |
|---|---|---|---|
| The aeroplane, the laboratory and the programmes flown on it | 73 | 21 | 28.8 percent |
| Simulation models, turbulence and the atmosphere | 76 | 19 | 25.0 percent |
| Stability, control effectiveness and the equations of motion | 233 | 55 | 23.6 percent |
| The measurement, being handling and flying qualities | 645 | 139 | 21.6 percent |
| The human being deceived, and the models made of that human | 307 | 61 | 19.9 percent |
| The cockpit, which is this aeroplane's own documented work | 369 | 72 | 19.5 percent |
| The instrument, being variable stability aeroplanes and in-flight simulation | 712 | 138 | 19.4 percent |
| Measuring any of it in the air | 216 | 35 | 16.2 percent |
| The hardware between the command and the aeroplane | 143 | 20 | 14.0 percent |
| Getting the model in the first place | 387 | 54 | 14.0 percent |
| The high angle of attack work this airframe did first | 375 | 51 | 13.6 percent |
| Designing the loop | 1,759 | 216 | 12.3 percent |
| The characteristic failure, being pilot-induced oscillation and rate limiting | 402 | 27 | 6.7 percent |
| Model following, which is the mathematics of pretending | 891 | 51 | 5.7 percent |
| The autonomy the X number was for | 412 | 20 | 4.9 percent |

**The keystone is the second thinnest cluster in the article and the publisher composition says why rather than excusing it.** Model following sits at 5.7 percent against the article's 14.0. Venues are counted here by name after setting aside years, punctuation, the abbreviations a society or conference prints beside its own name, the phrases `proceedings of` and `and Exhibit`, and the word `Navigation`, so that one conference filed under several names counts once, and every one of the cluster's 891 records is in the denominator, including the 66 that carry no venue. **On that rule one aeronautical society's guidance and control conference holds 11.9 percent of the cluster, and no other venue holds more than five percent of it.** The next are the American Control Conference at 4.7 percent, the same society's SciTech forum at 3.5, its own journal at 2.8 and a control-theory journal at 2.2. **It is a dispersed conference and journal literature and it was never a report literature**, which is a fact about where control theory publishes.

**The aeronautical half of the same subject is report literature and the contrast is the evidence.** In-flight simulation, which is model following carried out in an aeroplane rather than on paper, sits at 19.4 percent, 3.4 times the keystone's.

**The thinnest cluster is the autonomy the X number was for at 4.9 percent and the thickest is the aeroplane, the laboratory and the programmes flown on it at 28.8.**

### The Programme's Own Papers Form Two Sessions

**The programme published eight papers at the 2023 SciTech forum of the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics, and their identifiers fall in two contiguous blocks of four**, 1744 to 1747 and 1925 to 1928, which is the shape of two conference sessions. They cover the aeroplane's capabilities and architecture, the model-following algorithm and its control allocation, the design of the simulation system and its ground and flight testing, the design of the system for autonomous control of the simulation, the flight testing of the simulation and the autonomy, and a vision for accelerating autonomy test and evaluation on the aeroplane.

**The registry also records a correction notice on one of the eight**, which is a fact about the record rather than about the aeroplane. The article cites it and does not know what was corrected.

### The School Teaches the Scale Its Own Aeroplane Is Measured On

**The United States Air Force Test Pilot School publishes its Flying Qualities Phase textbook chapter by chapter into the defence registry.** **Chapter 16 is a reprint of NASA Technical Note D-5153**, which is Cooper and Harper's own paper defining the rating scale.

**It closes a loop between the aeroplane that produces the stimulus and the scale the answer is written on**, and it documents that loop in the school's own publication.

### What Was Read Rather Than Retrieved

**The contract analysis is computed from 79 raw transactions rather than from any stated total.** Each award's visible transactions are summed and compared with the amount the registry states separately, and 17 of the 18 agree to the cent. The remaining one is excluded because part of it falls past this article's date.

**The dateline horizon is enforced at the source and not in the prose.** 6 transactions carry an action date after 2025-12-07, of which 4 carry money totalling 782,854.00 dollars. **One of them is the only place in the entire record where the designation appears**, so an article that had filtered in the sentence rather than in the data would have reported the opposite of this record's most interesting property.

**Every published constant in the arithmetic comes from one NASA report that was downloaded and read.** Its Table 1 gives the mass, inertias, wing geometry and surface deflection limits, and its Appendix A gives the actuator lag and the rate limit of every surface but the speedbrake. **The report never names the aeroplane in its title** and states in its appendix on aerodynamic data that the data came from wind-tunnel tests of subscale models of the F-16.

**The programme's own technical papers are cited for their existence, their authorship and their subject.** Those are the facts the Crossref registry establishes, and each is stated as the registry records it. **Their contents are not quoted and their findings are not represented**, because this article has not read them.

**That is a limit of the available record rather than a preference.** Crossref carries an abstract for a great many works and an abstract is published metadata that may legitimately be read and quoted. **It carries none for any of the eight**, nor for the aeroplane's two founding papers of 1984 and 1988. The publisher deposits the title, the authors, the venue and the year and nothing else, so the registry route stops exactly where the article stops.

### Thin Subjects

**Six subjects that this article's derivations depend on have thin literatures.** Each count below is the number of research records in this survey whose title carries at least one of the listed terms. Where a row joins two groups of terms with the word together, a title must carry a term from each group.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---|
| the pseudoinverse and the projector of the matching condition | pseudoinverse, pseudo-inverse, generalized inverse, generalised inverse, projector, Moore-Penrose | 11 |
| a rate limit read as a corner frequency | rate limit, rate limiting, rate limited, rate limiter, rate saturation, rate saturating together with frequency, bandwidth, corner | 0 |
| the equivalent delay of an in-flight simulator | time delay, time delays, transport delay, latency, equivalent delay together with in-flight simulation, in-flight simulator, in-flight and ground-based simulation, variable stability, airborne simulator, airborne simulation | 2 |
| direct lift control | direct lift | 7 |
| statistics of pilot ratings | pilot rating, pilot ratings, Cooper-Harper, handling qualities rating, handling qualities ratings together with statistic, statistical, variability, ordinal, median, nonparametric, treatment | 4 |
| autonomy hosted on an in-flight simulator | in-flight simulation, in-flight simulator, variable stability, airborne simulator, VISTA, X-62 together with autonomy, autonomous, artificial intelligence, unmanned, uncrewed, agent | 1 |

**The algebra of the keystone is not a title subject.** Of the 11 titles that name a pseudoinverse, a generalised inverse or a projector, 8 concern allocation, 2 concern the reconfiguration of a flight control system and 1 applies a generalised inverse to model following, so the projector condition rests on the Technical Memorandum of 1967 and the linear algebra references rather than on a body of titles.

**A rate limit has a literature and a frequency has a literature, and their quotient has none.** No title in the survey pairs a rate limit with a frequency, a bandwidth or a corner, so the reading of a rate limit as a corner frequency, which decides where the simulation runs out of authority, rests on the published limits and on the arithmetic of the section headed Dependent Systems.

**The delay floor of an in-flight simulator is the subject of 2 titles**, both comparing manual control with added time delay in in-flight and ground-based simulation, so the floor this article derives from the actuator lag is bracketed by the literature rather than stated in it.

**Direct lift control, which is what the symmetric flap supplies, holds 7 titles**, so the claim that the flap is the missing column rests on the counting bound rather than on a literature of direct lift.

**The statistics of pilot ratings hold 4 titles**, 3 on the variability of ratings and 1 on the treatment of rating data, and none of them names an ordinal scale, a median or a nonparametric test, so the claim that a mean rating is a category error stands on the definition of the scale rather than on a published analysis of the practice.

**Autonomy hosted on an in-flight simulator holds 1 title**, an evaluation of the autonomous flying qualities of a simulated variable-stability aircraft \[[Hamidani and Kunz 2018][research_hamidani_kunz_2018]\].

**One conclusion of this article has no aeronautical literature at all, and it is reported as such rather than softened.** It is the claim that the contract record and the designation register are independent and here they agree. **That is a claim about records rather than about aeroplanes**, and it rests on the two records themselves, both of which are cited and both of which a reader can check.

### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject.** The subjects are those the argument uses, being model following and model-reference control of any plant, variable-stability aircraft and flight simulation, pilot-induced oscillation and actuator saturation, handling qualities and pilot rating, the human operator as a controller, this aeroplane and its programmes, autonomy for aircraft and the verification of autonomous systems, system identification, flight control design, cockpit displays, high angle of attack flight, actuators and digital delay, flight test, and stability and control. **General aerodynamics with no stability, control or flight dynamics content is not among them**, so airfoil and wing computation, aircraft performance, propulsion, aeroelasticity and flutter, loads and structures, and acoustics are excluded even where the vehicle is an aeroplane, and no cluster collects records that fit nowhere else.

**Several of this subject's words also name something else, and a record that shares only such a word is excluded.** The excluded literatures are road vehicles and their drivers, among them driving simulators and automotive head-up displays, together with clinical medicine and rehabilitation, robots and manipulators, ships and underwater vehicles, spacecraft attitude and orbit control, process, chemical, nuclear and power-system control, computer hard disk drives, coupled oscillators in physics and biology, railways, speech and audiology, agriculture, water treatment and batteries, and the biomechanics of rising from a chair. **Tracking studies whose subject is a drug, a toxicant, hypnosis, noise or brain activity rather than the operator's control behaviour are excluded**, because the argument uses the human operator as a controller. **Task allocation, command and control reference models and robot inverse dynamics share words with control allocation, reference models and dynamic inversion and are excluded as well.** Correction, erratum, retraction and withdrawal notices, decision letters, reviewer reports and author responses, and figure and supplementary-material records are excluded too, because a survey counts research works and those are parts of works or editorial events rather than works. A review of a book, a reference, glossary or definition entry, a notice such as an editorial or a news item, and a second deposit of a document already counted are not admitted either, since none of them is a research work in its own right.

**Three literatures that are contamination for other subjects are part of this one.** The human-factors literature of cockpit displays and symbology is on subject, because this subject is a pilot in a cockpit being deceived about which aeroplane is being flown, and the aircraft's own documented programme work is a programmable helmet-mounted display and a virtual head-up display. The curriculum literature of test pilot schools is on subject, because the aircraft is operated by a school and flown by its students. The physiology of pilot workload is on subject, because it is the discipline that measures a pilot, while clinical medicine is not.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept.** Model-reference and model-following control of plants other than aircraft, such as robots, reactors, power converters and a satellite, is kept because the method is the keystone. The verification and validation of autonomous ground, marine and space systems is kept beside the autonomy this aeroplane now hosts, and the handling qualities of spacecraft and lunar vehicles are kept because the measurement is the same. Each is kept, and a reader may weigh it accordingly.

**Every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.** A reading of titles cannot show that a work is relevant in substance, so this is a statement about titles only.

#### Five Words That Name Something Else

**Five of this subject's words collide severely with other literatures.**

**In the Crossref registry the bare word `VISTA` names chiefly Microsoft Windows Vista administration books**, together with the grammaticalisation of the Portuguese `em vista de` and place names, and nothing aeronautical among its leading results. Qualified as an in-flight simulator it names the aeroplane's own founding papers from 1984 and 1988. **The bare word therefore admits no record to this survey.**

**`Skyborg` cannot be qualified with `autonomy`.** In the registry that word names Spinoza on autonomy, contractual autonomy, the autonomy of labour law, autonomy and paternalism, and autonomy in schooling. **Autonomy is a word in political philosophy long before it is a word in aviation**, and it is one of the worst qualifiers available for this subject.

**`ACE` is the programme this aeroplane flew for and it collides with an economics subfield using the same three letters.** Agent-Based Computational Economics is abbreviated ACE and has its own journals and calls for papers. **The word `agent` makes it worse rather than better**, because a surface-active agent is an agent. The survey therefore admits the programme only by its full name.

**`Calspan` is a strong anchor and not a clean one**, because it is a whole laboratory, so the bare name in the registry also covers its shock tunnels, a Chrysler research safety vehicle and electromagnetic wave absorption alongside its variable-stability aircraft. **And `NF-16D` is an excellent anchor while `16D` alone is not**, the latter naming a Renaissance poem and a Nova Scotia map sheet.

**Two of this article's own words are internal homonyms, which is the most dangerous kind.** `Model following` shares a participle with terrain following, which is a different problem, and `simulation` means a computer program everywhere in engineering while here it means an aeroplane.

## Epistemic State

### What Is Assumed

**The short-period frequency against which the published rate limits are located.** 4 radians per second is a representative value for a fighter and not a measurement of any aeroplane this machine simulates. **The conclusion that the symmetric tail's full-deflection corner frequency is the lowest of the four does not depend on it**, because that is a ratio of two published numbers. **The conclusion that the tail is rate limited at the short period does depend on it**, and would fail for a model whose short period sat below 2.4 radians per second.

**The frame rate of the digital implementation.** Sixty hertz is assumed and is not known. It enters only the computational share of the delay floor. **The actuator's contribution of 49.5 milliseconds is published and is a floor on its own.**

**The separation between the two lifting controls' centres of pressure.** 0.6 chords is inferred from the published overall length and mean aerodynamic chord and from where a trailing-edge flap and a horizontal tail sit on an aeroplane of this layout. **The identity that the determinant is proportional to that separation does not depend on the value.** The condition numbers in the table beside it do, and are offered as a sensitivity rather than as a measurement.

**The host and model matrices in the worked residual.** These are representative short-period pairs. **The published F-16 aerodynamic data is tabular and graphical**, so this article has not computed the aeroplane's control effectiveness matrix. **What the worked example demonstrates is the asymmetry between the two rows**, which follows from a tail making moment and a flap making lift and would survive any plausible choice of numbers. **The deflection figures that follow from those matrices inherit the same status**, so the finding that the flap saturates before the tail describes the shape of the problem and does not measure this aeroplane.

**The crossover frequency of the pilot and vehicle loop.** Three and six radians per second are taken as a bracket for compensatory tracking, and no source read here states the range, so both ends are assumptions. **The phase the delay costs is proportional to that frequency**, so the percentages of margin consumed scale directly with an assumed quantity, and they are stated as a range for that reason. **The delay itself is published.**

**That an equivalent time delay is the right summary of the host's contribution.** The article checks the approximation rather than asserting it, finding the lag and a pure delay agreeing in phase to within about a seventh of a degree at four radians per second. **Above about eight radians per second the approximation begins to matter**, and the article makes no claim there.

**That the list of surfaces the second flight control system commands is correct.** **This input bears the most load in the article and has the weakest sourcing.** The counting bound, the rank deficits, the worked residual and the finding about which surface saturates all depend on a six-item list, and that list comes from two secondary web references which agree with one another \[[X-62A and NF-16D VISTA, GlobalSecurity.org][ref_gs_x62]\] \[[F-16 VISTA, MATV and NF-16D, Variable-stability In-flight Simulator Test Aircraft, F-16.net][ref_f16net_vista]\]. **Two independent secondary sources agreeing is better than one and is not a primary.** The programme's architecture paper almost certainly states it \[[Cotting et al. 2023b][ref_scitech_capabilities]\], and this article has not read it and will not paraphrase it. **If that list is wrong in any one entry, the axis it belongs to loses a column and the projector stops vanishing**. No single correction would do more damage to what follows.

**That the register's engines cell and the block convention are both correct.** The resolution offered is that the aeroplane was re-engined, which two independent sources state. **No source this article found addresses the inlet, the part of an engine change a block number encodes.**

### What Is Computed

**The model-following conditions and the projector.** The condition for exact model following, the gains when it holds, the residual when it does not, the error dynamics that residual drives, the steady error those dynamics settle to, and the rank bound that turns all of it into a count of control surfaces. **These are algebra and carry no empirical content beyond the linearity of the two systems.** The weaker condition for matching an output rather than a state is algebra of the same kind, and it appears here because it shows the counting bound to be sufficient rather than necessary.

**The two short periods as modes.** The natural frequency and damping of the host and the divergent root and time to double of the model, from the trace and determinant of each matrix.

**The deflections the worked simulation demands**, from the gains that solve the matching condition, together with the angle of attack at which each surface reaches its published limit and the bound the smallest singular value places on the whole gain matrix.

**The describing-function gain of a rate limiter in deep saturation**, from the triangular output such an element produces and the known fundamental of a triangular wave. **The phase is not computed and is not quoted**, for the reason the section gives.

**The phase margin a delay consumes at a given crossover**, from the integrator of the crossover model, and the frequency at which it consumes all of it.

**The leading-edge flap schedule and the actuator in series**, from the transfer functions the report prints, including the product of the schedule's pole and the actuator's time constant.

**The invariance of the median and the non-invariance of the mean** under a strictly increasing relabelling, the formal content of the claim that a mean rating is a category error.

**The rank deficits by axis**, from the published list of surfaces the second flight control system commands and the standard decomposition of aircraft dynamics into three dynamic states per axis.

**The worked residual**, including the row-wise fractions of 83.3 percent and 0.05 percent and their ratio of 1,677.

**The determinant identity and the condition numbers**, from geometry alone.

**Every corner frequency in the limits table**, from the deflection and rate limits published in NASA Technical Paper 1538, together with the usable fractions at the assumed short-period frequency.

**The actuator corner frequency, its phase contribution and the equivalent delay**, from the published lag.

**Every figure in the contract analysis**, summed from the transaction record rather than read from a stated total, with 17 of 18 awards agreeing to the cent with the total the registry states separately.

**Every figure about the register**, computed from the register's table, including the count of rows containing the word `redesignated` and the ranking of this row's description length.

### What the Record Does Not Settle

**Why the leading-edge flap is not commanded by the second flight control system.** The article offers three reasons, being the surface's slow actuator, its low full-deflection corner frequency, and the fact that it is already carrying a scheduled command whose lead its actuator very nearly cancels. **No source consulted states which of the three governed, or whether the question was ever asked.**

**Whether the near-coincidence of the flap schedule's pole and the flap actuator's corner is deliberate.** They differ by 1.42 percent. **A schedule designed for an aeroplane and an actuator sized for a surface may arrive at the same corner frequency by accident**, and this article reports the coincidence and claims nothing about its cause.

**The phase a rate-limited actuator contributes.** An ideal rate limiter contributes none. A rate-limited servo contributes up to a great deal, and how much depends on the loop around the limiter. **This article has the limit and the lag and does not have the loop.**

**Whether the change in how the acronym is expanded was deliberate.** The award record uses the older form and the prime contractor uses the newer one. **That the newer form spells the acronym exactly and the older one does not is arithmetic. That anyone noticed is conjecture.**

**What inlet the aircraft carries.** See above.

**The frame rate, the computational latency and the actual model-following architecture.** The programme has published on all three, in eight conference papers \[[Cotting et al. 2023b][ref_scitech_capabilities]\] \[[Caraway et al. 2023][ref_scitech_mfa]\] \[[Harris and Caraway 2023][ref_scitech_allocation]\], and **this article cites all eight as registry entries, which establish that they exist, who wrote them and what they cover.** It does not quote their contents and does not represent their findings. **The registry also records a correction to one of them** \[[Correction to X-62 VISTA Simulation and Autonomy Flight Testing, AIAA SciTech 2023][ref_scitech_flight_testing_correction]\]. The correction is a fact about the record rather than about the aeroplane, and this article reports it without knowing what was corrected.

**The phase-delay parameter of the bandwidth criterion.** It is how the field expresses what the delay floor costs, and the article declines to use it because a derivation from an unverified statement of its definition gives half what the usual summary of the subject states. **A factor of two on the one quantity the criterion would have supplied is not a rounding**, and the specification that settles it has not been read.

**How widely pilot ratings are averaged in practice.** The scale's definition forbids it. **Measuring how often the field does it anyway would require a reading of the literature this survey has not performed.**

**Whether the aeroplane's actuators have been changed since 1979.** The rate limits used here are those of a production F-16 as NASA modelled it. Its variable-stability modification added a larger-capacity hydraulic pump and lines to accommodate the increased surface motions \[[F-16 VISTA, MATV and NF-16D, Variable-stability In-flight Simulator Test Aircraft, F-16.net][ref_f16net_vista]\], so **an aeroplane that has been modified as often as this one may well no longer match them**, and no source consulted states the current values. **Every frequency in this article's rate-limit argument inherits that uncertainty**, and the direction of the error is not known.

## Out of Scope

**The aeroplane's performance is out of scope.** Its span, wing area, engine and performance are those of an F-16D and are tabulated in the ordinary reference works \[[General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon][ref_f16]\], and The Research Question gives the reason this article does not reproduce them.

**The airframe's earlier research programmes are out of scope as programmes.** The thrust-vectoring work of the early nineteen nineties appears only as the history that explains the engines cell, and the high angle of attack literature that work belongs to is listed under The Contemporary Literature without being argued.

**The contents of the programme's own technical papers are out of scope**, because this article has not read them. It cites them only to establish that they exist, who wrote them and what they address.

**Two quantities the field would expect are out of scope by decision.** The bandwidth criterion and its phase-delay parameter are not used, for the reason given under Why the Bandwidth Criterion Is Not Used, and the phase a rate-limited servo contributes is not quoted, because the article has the actuator's limit and lag and not its loop.

**The conduct and outcome of the autonomy engagements are out of scope** beyond what the agency, the prime contractor and the trade press state, and the article reports those statements as claims. **So is the inlet the aeroplane now carries**, which no source this article found addresses.

## Conclusion

**Of the five orderings between a designation and its aeroplane that this series has met, the X-62A's is the only one in which the number records a change of purpose rather than an event in the aeroplane's life.** What changed in June 2021 was what the machine was lying to.

For twenty-nine years it lied to pilots. It was an NF-16D, a status prefix meaning that undoing the modifications is beyond practicable or economic limits. It supported the development of the F-22 and of India's Light Combat Aircraft and evaluated the flight characteristics of aircraft that had not yet flown \[[X-62A and NF-16D VISTA, GlobalSecurity.org][ref_gs_x62]\], and it made a Block 30 F-16D behave like an aeroplane with flying qualities bad enough to be dangerous and a safety pilot in the back seat to make that survivable. **In June 2021 it became an X-plane, and the thing it lies to now is software.**

**The mathematics of the lie is exact and older than the aeroplane.** One linear system can be made to reproduce another if and only if a projector built from the host's control effectiveness matrix annihilates the demanded change of dynamics. **When it does, the gains are immediate and the imitation is perfect. When it does not, the residual is computable, it is driven by the model's state, and no feedback gain removes it.** The condition is about how many independent directions the host's controls can reach, and it turns the design of an in-flight simulator into a counting problem.

**The count comes out at three per axis and the aeroplane has three per axis.** A symmetric horizontal tail, a symmetric trailing-edge flap and a throttle in pitch. A differential tail, an aileron and a rudder in roll and yaw. **The throttle is in the list because the speed equation is one of the three and no commanded surface can change axial force independently**. This article found no clearer illustration of the argument removing the vehicle. **The engine appears in the mathematics as a column and not as propulsion.**

**And the same argument says what a simulator built round one pitch control could and could not do.** It could retune pitch stiffness and pitch damping almost exactly. **It could not change the lift curve at all**, and the ratio between those two failures, in a representative case, is 1,677. A variable-stability aeroplane without a direct lift control can imitate a different tail and cannot imitate a different wing. **The error it would leave does not decay**, because the model's state drives the residual and no gain appears in it to tune.

**Solving the same example for its deflections rather than its residual reverses an intuition.** The tail is the powerful surface and the flap is the afterthought, and the counting bound says only that the flap must be present. **The flap is what runs out.** It reaches its published limit at 8.17 degrees of angle of attack where the tail would not reach its own until 30.5, so **the envelope of aeroplanes this machine can imitate is set by its weakest control and not by its strongest.**

**The limits that bind in practice are published and have been since 1979.** The symmetric horizontal tail, which has the most travel of any pitch surface the second system commands, reaches its stops only below 2.4 radians per second, below a fighter's short-period frequency. **The differential tail, with a fifth of the travel and the same rate limit, has 4.65 times the bandwidth.** The rate limits were set for a fighter, published twelve years before the simulator flew, and inherited unevenly, with the worst of it falling on the axis that does most of the work.

**The deepest limit is one-sided and no software will move it.** A model-following system drives the host's surfaces, so every delay in the host lies between the pilot and the simulated response, and the simulation can only add. **The machine can make any aeroplane sluggish and cannot make any aeroplane crisp.** The floor is at least 49.5 milliseconds from the published actuator lag alone.

**And the instrument contains the nonlinearity it was built to study.** Rate limiting is a recognised mechanism of pilot-induced oscillation \[[Pilot-induced oscillation][ref_pio]\], and the second flight control system drives the same surfaces through what this article takes to be the same rate limits. **Above the published corners the host contributes a further nonlinearity**, and the student cannot tell it from the model's. A rate limiter in deep saturation returns a triangular wave whose fundamental falls as the reciprocal of both amplitude and frequency, **so the harder the pilot works the less of the aeroplane comes back**, the positive feedback the phenomenon runs on.

**The delay floor can be priced in the currency the pilot spends.** A trained operator adapts until the open loop is an integrator at crossover, which leaves ninety degrees of margin, and a transport delay takes from that linearly. **At three radians per second the host consumes 14.23 percent of it and at six it consumes 28.46 percent**, before the simulated aeroplane has contributed anything at all.

**And a surface the simulation might have wanted turns out to be spoken for.** The leading-edge flap is a direct lift device and would be a fourth column in the longitudinal matrix, and the second system does not command it. The published schedule that does command it asks for a lead of two above 3.625 radians per second, **and the flap actuator's corner sits 1.42 percent from the schedule's pole**, so across the band where the simulation lives the surface delivers a gain rise of 0.8 where the schedule asks for 1.8. **The lead is not merely reduced. Its sign is reversed.**

**The answer then comes back on a scale with ten boxes and no metric.** The Cooper-Harper rating is ordinal by construction, its only claims about magnitude are the two level boundaries, and a statistic is meaningful on such a scale exactly when it survives every strictly increasing relabelling of the boxes. **The median does and the mean does not**, so a mean of such ratings asserts something the scale declines to supply. **The instrument is far more precise than its readout.**

**And the loop between the instrument and the readout is closed inside one institution.** The school that flies this aeroplane publishes its own flying-qualities textbook chapter by chapter into the defence registry, **and Chapter 16 of that textbook is a reprint of the paper that defines the rating scale.** The aeroplane produces the stimulus, the student produces the rating, and the definition of the rating is bound into the curriculum the student was taught from. **A scale taught as a chapter is a scale applied consistently, and consistency is not the same thing as an interval.**

**The money says what all of this costs and never once says what the aeroplane is called.** 73 transactions and 29,085,924.37 dollars over 11.6 years, 81.2 percent of it to the laboratory that owns the simulation system and 18.8 percent to the prime contractor that owns the airframe and the autonomy interface. **The obligation rate steps by a factor of 3.17 at the redesignation** and the first payment lands 31 days after it. **And in 73 transactions the string X-62A appears 0 times.**

**That absence is the article's opening finding and it returns here at the close because it is no clerical curiosity.** A designation is a claim about a vehicle's purpose, made by one part of a government to another. **The part that buys the fuel and the spares had no use for the claim**, because for its purposes the aeroplane had not changed and the contract line was the same contract line. **Both records are right. They are answering different questions.**

**The register's sentence is not official wording and the compiler marks it as reconstructed, yet the accounting system corroborates it.** Three months after the redesignation the Air Force obligated 799,956.00 dollars under a line that names the Skyborg programme. **The two records are maintained for unrelated purposes and they agree.** That agreement is the strongest thing this series has been able to say about a reconstructed description since the register stopped being a primary source one article ago.

**What the next article inherits is a register that has now been unofficial for two designations running**, and the X-63A, allocated 10.2 months after this one, is the third \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\].

## Equations

<!-- Equations generated by _lib/equations.py from _sources/equations/. Edit the data file and regenerate. Do not edit this section by hand. -->

This section collects the 55 display equations of the article in the order they appear,
each under its number and reproduced exactly as it stands in the text.
A title in bold names an established result,
and a title in italics beginning with the word Bespoke names a construction made for this analysis.
Of the 55, 42 are established and 13 are bespoke.
The dynamics matrices are in inverse seconds and carry representative rather than measured values, surface deflections and rates are evaluated in degrees and degrees per second although the notation key states radians, and several letters depart from their usual meanings, so $e$ is the model-following state error while $e^{- \tau s}$ is the exponential of a delay, $P_s$ is the static pressure and not a specific excess power, $\gamma$ is a deflection gradient and not a ratio of specific heats, $g$ is a relabelling of the rating scale and not gravity, $A$ is a generic two-by-two matrix in the trace and determinant relation, and $V$ and $v$ are obligations in dollars.

*Equation 1, Bespoke Fraction of the Flying Life Carried Under an X Number.*
The article defines the share of the aeroplane's life as the Variable Stability In-flight Simulator Test Aircraft, VISTA, that it has flown with an X designation, measured from the first flight and the designation date to the date of the article.
[General Dynamics X-62 VISTA][ref_x62_wikipedia]
[Flight Test Files, Viper X, Vintage Aviation News][ref_vintage_viper_x]
[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]

$$
F = \frac{T_n - T_d}{T_n - T_0}
\tag{1}
$$

**Equation 2, Transactions Sum to the Award Total.**
The obligations of an award's transactions, filed one at a time, sum to the separately stated award total.
[USAspending][ref_usaspending]

$$
\sum_k v_k = V
\tag{2}
$$

**Equation 3, Contractor Shares of the Recorded Obligation.**
Each contractor's share is its subtotal divided by the whole record, giving Calspan 81.2 percent and Lockheed Martin 18.8 percent.

$$
\rho_p = \frac{V_p}{V_{\text{all}}} , \qquad \rho_{\text{Calspan}} = \frac{23{,}611{,}921.77}{29{,}085{,}924.37} = 0.812 , \qquad \rho_{\text{Lockheed Martin}} = \frac{5{,}474{,}002.60}{29{,}085{,}924.37} = 0.188
\tag{3}
$$

**Equation 4, Symmetric and Differential Tail Commands.**
The symmetric and differential commands are an invertible change of basis on the left and right tail deflections, so the pair supplies two independent controls.

$$
\begin{bmatrix} \delta_s \\ \delta_d \end{bmatrix} = \tfrac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \delta_L \\ \delta_R \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \det = - \tfrac{1}{2} \ne 0
\tag{4}
$$

**Equation 5, Linear Models of the Host and the Simulated Aeroplane.**
The host and the model are each a linear state-space system with its own dynamics and control effectiveness matrices.
[Stevens, Lewis and Johnson, Aircraft Control and Simulation][book_stevens_lewis]
[McRuer, Ashkenas and Graham, Aircraft Dynamics and Automatic Control][book_mcruer_dynamics]

$$
\dot{x} = A x + B u , \qquad \dot{x}_m = A_m x_m + B_m u_m
\tag{5}
$$

**Equation 6, Model-Following Control Law.**
The host's controls are a linear combination of its own state, the model's state and the model's control input.
[Model reference adaptive control][ref_mrac]

$$
u = K_x x + K_m x_m + K_u u_m
\tag{6}
$$

**Equation 7, Closed Loop Under Model Following.**
Substituting the control law into the host's dynamics gives the closed-loop state equation.

$$
\dot{x} = \left( A + B K_x \right) x + B K_m x_m + B K_u u_m
\tag{7}
$$

**Equation 8, Matching Conditions on the Gains.**
For the host to follow the model exactly, the closed loop must equal the model term by term, which gives two linear conditions on the gains.

$$
B \left( K_x + K_m \right) = A_m - A , \qquad B K_u = B_m
\tag{8}
$$

**Equation 9, Projector Onto the Unreachable Subspace.**
The identity minus the control matrix times its Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse projects onto the complement of the column space of the control matrix.
[Moore-Penrose inverse][ref_pseudoinverse]
[Projection, the linear algebraic operation][ref_projection]

$$
\Pi = I - B B^{+}
\tag{9}
$$

**Equation 10, Erzberger Conditions for Perfect Model Following.**
Exact model following is possible if and only if the projector annihilates both the demanded change of dynamics and the model's control matrix.
[Erzberger, Analysis and Design of Model Following Control Systems by State Space Techniques, NASA Technical Memorandum X-61189, 18 October 1967][ref_erzberger_1967]

$$
\Pi \left( A_m - A \right) = 0 , \qquad \Pi B_m = 0
\tag{10}
$$

**Equation 11, Least-Squares Model-Following Gains.**
When the conditions hold, the gains are the pseudoinverse solutions of the matching conditions, which are then exact.
[Erzberger, Analysis and Design of Model Following Control Systems by State Space Techniques, NASA Technical Memorandum X-61189, 18 October 1967][ref_erzberger_1967]
[Asseo, Application of Optimal Control to Perfect Model Following, Journal of Aircraft, 1970][ref_asseo_1970]

$$
K_x + K_m = B^{+} \left( A_m - A \right) , \qquad K_u = B^{+} B_m
\tag{11}
$$

**Equation 12, Demanded Change of Dynamics.**
The change of dynamics a simulation demands is the model's dynamics matrix less the host's.

$$
\Delta A = A_m - A
\tag{12}
$$

**Equation 13, Unmatchable Residual.**
The part of the demanded change that the projector leaves is the residual no control law can produce.

$$
E = \Pi \left( A_m - A \right)
\tag{13}
$$

**Equation 14, Model-Following Error Dynamics.**
The state error between host and model obeys a stable homogeneous response driven by the residual acting on the model's state and by any mismatch in the input gains.
[Anderson and Schmidt, Error Dynamics and Perfect Model Following With Application to Flight Control, Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics, 1991][ref_anderson_1991]

$$
\dot{e} = \left( A + B K_x \right) e + E x_m + \left( B K_u - B_m \right) u_m
\tag{14}
$$

**Equation 15, Steady Model-Following Error.**
Setting the error derivative to zero gives a steady error that depends on the residual and the model's state and that no choice of feedback gain removes.
[Anderson and Schmidt, Error Dynamics and Perfect Model Following With Application to Flight Control, Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics, 1991][ref_anderson_1991]

$$
\dot{e} = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad e_\infty = - \left( A + B K_x \right)^{-1} \Pi \, \Delta A \, x_m
\tag{15}
$$

**Equation 16, Rank of the Projector.**
The rank of the projector is the number of states less the rank of the control matrix, and so at least the number of states less the number of controls.

$$
\operatorname{rank} \Pi = n - \operatorname{rank} B \; \ge \; n - m
\tag{16}
$$

**Equation 17, Output Model-Following Condition.**
Matching an output rather than the full state replaces the projector with one built from the product of the output and control matrices.
[Stevens, Lewis and Johnson, Aircraft Control and Simulation][book_stevens_lewis]

$$
y = C x \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \left( I - \left( C B \right) \left( C B \right)^{+} \right) C \, \Delta A = 0
\tag{17}
$$

**Equation 18, Short-Period Equations of Motion.**
The short period in angle of attack and pitch rate is a two-by-two linear system with the pitch-rate coefficient of the angle-of-attack equation normalised to unity.
[Etkin and Reid, Dynamics of Flight, Stability and Control][book_etkin_reid]
[Cook, Flight Dynamics Principles][book_cook]
[USAF Test Pilot School, Flying Qualities Phase, Chapter 4, Equations of Motion][ref_tps_ch4]
[USAF Test Pilot School, Flying Qualities Phase, Chapter 8, Dynamics][ref_tps_ch8]

$$
\begin{bmatrix} \dot{\alpha} \\ \dot{q} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} Z_\alpha & 1 \\ M_\alpha & M_q \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \alpha \\ q \end{bmatrix}
\tag{18}
$$

**Equation 19, Natural Frequency and Damping From the Trace and Determinant.**
For a two-by-two dynamics matrix the natural frequency is the square root of the determinant and twice the damping times the frequency is minus the trace.

$$
\omega_n = \sqrt{\det A} , \qquad 2 \zeta \omega_n = - \operatorname{tr} A
\tag{19}
$$

*Equation 20, Bespoke Host, Model and Control Matrices.*
The host, the model and the two pitch controls are representative short-period matrices chosen to make the arithmetic legible, with a tail column that makes much more moment than lift and a flap column the reverse.
[Nguyen, Ogburn, Gilbert, Kibler, Brown and Deal, Simulator Study of Stall and Post-Stall Characteristics of a Fighter Airplane With Relaxed Longitudinal Static Stability, NASA Technical Paper 1538, December 1979][ref_tp1538]

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix} -1.20 & 1.00 \\ -8.00 & -1.50 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad A_m = \begin{bmatrix} -0.60 & 1.00 \\ 2.00 & -0.40 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix} -0.09 & -0.20 \\ -9.00 & -1.00 \end{bmatrix}
\tag{20}
$$

**Equation 21, Divergent Root and Time to Double.**
A negative determinant gives a positive real eigenvalue, and the time to double amplitude is the natural logarithm of two divided by it.
[USAF Test Pilot School, Flying Qualities Phase, Chapter 5, Longitudinal Static Stability][ref_tps_ch5]

$$
\det A < 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \lambda = \tfrac{1}{2} \left( \operatorname{tr} A + \sqrt{\operatorname{tr}^2 A - 4 \det A} \right) > 0 , \qquad t_2 = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}
\tag{21}
$$

**Equation 22, Projector for a Single Control Column.**
With one control column the projector removes the direction of that column and leaves the perpendicular subspace untouched.

$$
\Pi = I - \frac{b \, b^{\mathrm{T}}}{b^{\mathrm{T}} b}
\tag{22}
$$

*Equation 23, Bespoke Unreachable Fraction of Each Row.*
The article defines, for each row of the demanded change, the norm of the residual over the norm of the demanded change as the fraction no control law can produce.

$$
\eta_\alpha = \frac{\left\| \left( \Pi \, \Delta A \right)_\alpha \right\|}{\left\| \Delta A_\alpha \right\|} , \qquad \eta_q = \frac{\left\| \left( \Pi \, \Delta A \right)_q \right\|}{\left\| \Delta A_q \right\|}
\tag{23}
$$

**Equation 24, Normal Load Factor per Unit Angle of Attack.**
The load factor a given angle of attack produces is the dynamic pressure times the wing area and lift-curve slope, divided by the weight.

$$
\frac{n_z}{\alpha} = \frac{\bar{q} \, S \, C_{L_\alpha}}{W}
\tag{24}
$$

**Equation 25, Pitching Moment of a Lifting Surface.**
A surface that produces a normal force aft of the centre of gravity produces a pitching moment proportional to it, with the arm measured in mean aerodynamic chords.
[Etkin and Reid, Dynamics of Flight, Stability and Control][book_etkin_reid]
[Nelson, Flight Stability and Automatic Control][book_nelson]

$$
M_f = - \frac{\ell_f}{\bar{c}} Z_f , \qquad M_h = - \frac{\ell_h}{\bar{c}} Z_h
\tag{25}
$$

**Equation 26, Determinant of Two Lifting Controls.**
The determinant of the block mapping two lifting controls onto normal force and pitching moment is the product of their effectivenesses times the difference of their stations.

$$
\det \begin{bmatrix} Z_f & Z_h \\ M_f & M_h \end{bmatrix} = \frac{Z_f Z_h}{\bar{c}} \left( \ell_f - \ell_h \right)
\tag{26}
$$

**Equation 27, Condition Number.**
The condition number of a matrix is its largest singular value divided by its smallest.
[Condition number][ref_condition_number]
[Singular value decomposition][ref_singular_value]

$$
\kappa = \frac{\sigma_{\max}}{\sigma_{\min}}
\tag{27}
$$

**Equation 28, Gain Bound From the Smallest Singular Value.**
The matching gains, and so the deflections they command, are bounded by the norm of the demanded change divided by the smallest singular value of the control matrix.

$$
u = \left( K_x + K_m \right) x , \qquad \left\| K_x + K_m \right\| \le \frac{\left\| \Delta A \right\|}{\sigma_{\min} \left( B \right)}
\tag{28}
$$

*Equation 29, Bespoke Deflection Gradients in the Worked Simulation.*
Solving the matching condition with the representative host, model and control matrices gives the symmetric tail and flap deflection per unit angle of attack.

$$
\Delta A = A_m - A = \begin{bmatrix} 0.60 & 0 \\ 10.00 & 1.10 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \begin{bmatrix} \gamma_s \\ \gamma_f \end{bmatrix} = B^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 0.60 \\ 10.00 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{-1.71} \begin{bmatrix} -1.00 & 0.20 \\ 9.00 & -0.09 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0.60 \\ 10.00 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -0.8187 \\ -2.6316 \end{bmatrix}
\tag{29}
$$

*Equation 30, Bespoke Saturation Angles of Attack.*
The representative deflection gradients are carried against the published limits of 25 degrees for the tail and 21.5 degrees for the flap, so the flap saturates first, at 8.17 degrees of angle of attack.
[Nguyen, Ogburn, Gilbert, Kibler, Brown and Deal, Simulator Study of Stall and Post-Stall Characteristics of a Fighter Airplane With Relaxed Longitudinal Static Stability, NASA Technical Paper 1538, December 1979][ref_tp1538]

$$
\delta = \left| \gamma \right| \alpha , \qquad \alpha_{\text{sat}} = \frac{\delta_{\max}}{\left| \gamma \right|} , \qquad \frac{21.5}{2.6316} = 8.17 , \qquad \frac{25}{0.8187} = 30.5 , \qquad \frac{2.6316 \times 5 / 21.5}{0.8187 \times 5 / 25} = \frac{0.6120}{0.1637} = 3.74
\tag{30}
$$

**Equation 31, Peak Rate of a Sinusoidal Deflection.**
A sinusoidal deflection moves fastest through zero at the amplitude times the frequency, which must not exceed the rate limit.
[Slew rate][ref_slew_rate]

$$
\delta \left( t \right) = \hat{\delta} \sin \omega t \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \left| \dot{\delta} \right|_{\max} = \hat{\delta} \omega \le R
\tag{31}
$$

*Equation 32, Bespoke Full-Deflection Corner Frequency.*
The article defines the corner frequency of a surface as its rate limit divided by its deflection limit, the highest frequency at which it can still reach its stops.

$$
\omega_c = \frac{R}{\delta_{\max}}
\tag{32}
$$

*Equation 33, Bespoke Fraction of Authority Available at a Frequency.*
Above the article's corner frequency the usable amplitude falls as the reciprocal of frequency, so the available fraction of travel is the lesser of one and the corner frequency over the frequency.
[Describing function][ref_describing_function]

$$
\frac{\hat{\delta} \left( \omega \right)}{\delta_{\max}} = \min \left( 1 , \frac{\omega_c}{\omega} \right)
\tag{33}
$$

*Equation 34, Bespoke Fraction of Authority at the Short Period.*
At the short-period frequency a surface whose corner frequency lies below it reaches only the ratio of the two frequencies of its travel.

$$
\frac{\hat{\delta} \left( \omega_{sp} \right)}{\delta_{\max}} = \frac{\omega_c}{\omega_{sp}} \qquad \text{whenever} \qquad \omega_c < \omega_{sp}
\tag{34}
$$

*Equation 35, Bespoke Stabilator Authority at a Representative Short Period.*
The published rate limit of 60 degrees per second and deflection limit of 25 degrees give a corner of 2.40 radians per second, which at a short period the article assumes to be 4 radians per second leaves 60 percent of the travel.

$$
\omega_c = \frac{60}{25} = 2.40 , \qquad \frac{\omega_c}{2 \pi} = 0.382 , \qquad \frac{\hat{\delta} \left( \omega_{sp} \right)}{\delta_{\max}} = \frac{2.40}{4} = 0.60 , \qquad \hat{\delta} = 0.60 \times 25 = 15
\tag{35}
$$

*Equation 36, Bespoke Ratio of Differential to Symmetric Tail Corner Frequencies.*
With a common rate limit, the ratio of the two corner frequencies is the inverse ratio of the published deflection limits.

$$
\frac{\omega_{c,d}}{\omega_{c,s}} = \frac{R / 5.375}{R / 25.0} = \frac{25.0}{5.375} = 4.65 , \qquad \frac{11.16}{2.40} = 4.65
\tag{36}
$$

*Equation 37, Bespoke Leading-Edge Flap Corner, Lag Ratio and Authority.*
The published travel and rate give the leading-edge flap a corner of one radian per second and an actuator lag 2.75 times the others, and at the assumed short period of 4 radians per second it reaches a quarter of its travel.
[Nguyen, Ogburn, Gilbert, Kibler, Brown and Deal, Simulator Study of Stall and Post-Stall Characteristics of a Fighter Airplane With Relaxed Longitudinal Static Stability, NASA Technical Paper 1538, December 1979][ref_tp1538]

$$
\omega_c = \frac{25.0}{25.0} = 1.00 , \qquad \frac{\tau_l}{\tau} = \frac{0.136}{0.0495} = 2.75 , \qquad \frac{\hat{\delta} \left( \omega_{sp} \right)}{\delta_{\max}} = \frac{1.00}{4} = 0.25
\tag{37}
$$

**Equation 38, Published Leading-Edge Flap Schedule.**
The leading-edge flap is scheduled by a lead network on angle of attack, a term in the ratio of dynamic to static pressure and a constant bias.
[Nguyen, Ogburn, Gilbert, Kibler, Brown and Deal, Simulator Study of Stall and Post-Stall Characteristics of a Fighter Airplane With Relaxed Longitudinal Static Stability, NASA Technical Paper 1538, December 1979][ref_tp1538]

$$
\delta_l = 1.38 \, \frac{2 s + \omega_p}{s + \omega_p} \, \alpha - 9.05 \, \frac{\bar{q}}{P_s} + 1.45 , \qquad \omega_p = 7.25
\tag{38}
$$

**Equation 39, Leading-Edge Flap Schedule in Series With Its Actuator.**
Putting the published schedule in series with the published first-order actuator lag gives the surface's response to angle of attack, with the schedule pole and actuator corner nearly coincident.

$$
\frac{\delta_l \left( s \right)}{\alpha \left( s \right)} = 1.38 \, \frac{2 s + \omega_p}{s + \omega_p} \cdot \frac{1}{\tau_l s + 1} , \qquad \omega_p \tau_l = 0.986
\tag{39}
$$

**Equation 40, Gain and Phase of the Series Response.**
Evaluating the series transfer function on the imaginary axis gives its magnitude and phase as functions of frequency.

$$
\left| \frac{\delta_l}{\alpha} \left( j \omega \right) \right| = 1.38 \, \frac{\sqrt{4 \omega^2 + \omega_p^2}}{\sqrt{\omega^2 + \omega_p^2}} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau_l^2 \omega^2 + 1}} , \qquad \varphi \left( \omega \right) = \arctan \frac{2 \omega}{\omega_p} - \arctan \frac{\omega}{\omega_p} - \arctan \tau_l \omega
\tag{40}
$$

**Equation 41, Gain Rises and Phase at Fifteen Radians per Second.**
The magnitudes at fifteen and at one radian per second, with and without the actuator factor, give the gain rises and the phase of the series response.

$$
\frac{1.853}{1.028} = 1.80 , \qquad \frac{1.853 \times 0.440}{1.028 \times 0.991} = 0.80 , \qquad \frac{1.80}{0.80} = 2.25 , \qquad \varphi \left( 15 \right) = 76.4 - 64.2 - 63.9 = - 51.7 \ \text{degrees}
\tag{41}
$$

**Equation 42, First-Order Actuator Lag.**
Every surface but the leading-edge flap follows its command through a first-order lag of the published time constant, with a corner at its reciprocal.
[Nguyen, Ogburn, Gilbert, Kibler, Brown and Deal, Simulator Study of Stall and Post-Stall Characteristics of a Fighter Airplane With Relaxed Longitudinal Static Stability, NASA Technical Paper 1538, December 1979][ref_tp1538]

$$
\frac{\delta \left( s \right)}{\delta_c \left( s \right)} = \frac{1}{\tau s + 1} , \qquad \omega_a = \frac{1}{\tau}
\tag{42}
$$

**Equation 43, Phase of a First-Order Lag.**
The phase of a first-order lag is minus the arctangent of the frequency times the time constant.

$$
\varphi \left( \omega \right) = - \arctan \left( \omega \tau \right)
\tag{43}
$$

**Equation 44, First-Order Lag as a Pure Delay at Low Frequency.**
At frequencies well below its corner a first-order lag behaves as a pure time delay of the same time constant.

$$
\frac{1}{\tau s + 1} \; \simeq \; e^{- \tau s} \qquad \text{whenever} \qquad \omega \tau \ll 1
\tag{44}
$$

**Equation 45, Equivalent Delays in Series Add.**
The equivalent delay of a host and a model in series is the sum of their delays, and so is never less than the host's alone.

$$
\tau_e \left( \text{host and model} \right) = \tau_e \left( \text{host} \right) + \tau_e \left( \text{model} \right) \; \ge \; \tau_e \left( \text{host} \right)
\tag{45}
$$

*Equation 46, Bespoke Floor on the Simulated Delay.*
The article bounds the delay a pilot meets below by the actuator lag plus half a frame of sampling and one frame of transport, an implementation it assumes.

$$
\tau_s \; \ge \; \tau + \frac{3}{2 f_s}
\tag{46}
$$

**Equation 47, Output Amplitude of a Saturated Rate Limiter.**
A rate limiter deep in saturation produces a triangular wave whose amplitude follows from the rate limit and the frequency alone.
[Describing function][ref_describing_function]
[Slotine and Li, Applied Nonlinear Control][book_slotine]

$$
\left| \dot{\delta} \right| = R \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \hat{\delta}_o = \frac{\pi R}{2 \omega}
\tag{47}
$$

**Equation 48, Describing Function of a Saturated Rate Limiter.**
The fundamental of the triangular output divided by the input amplitude gives a gain that falls with both frequency and amplitude.
[Describing function][ref_describing_function]
[Slotine and Li, Applied Nonlinear Control][book_slotine]

$$
\left| N \right| = \frac{8}{\pi^2} \cdot \frac{\hat{\delta}_o}{\hat{\delta}} = \frac{4 R}{\pi \, \hat{\delta} \, \omega}
\tag{48}
$$

**Equation 49, McRuer Crossover Model.**
A trained pilot adapts until the combined pilot and vehicle open loop looks like an integrator with a delay near the crossover frequency.
[McRuer and Krendel, Mathematical Models of Human Pilot Behavior][book_mcruer_pilot]
[McRuer, Ashkenas and Graham, Aircraft Dynamics and Automatic Control][book_mcruer_dynamics]

$$
Y_p \left( s \right) Y_c \left( s \right) \; \simeq \; \frac{\omega_{co} \, e^{- \tau_e s}}{s}
\tag{49}
$$

**Equation 50, Phase Margin of the Crossover Model.**
The crossover model leaves ninety degrees of margin less the phase the effective delay costs at crossover.

$$
\varphi_m = \frac{\pi}{2} - \omega_{co} \tau_e
\tag{50}
$$

*Equation 51, Bespoke Share of the Margin Consumed by the Delay Floor.*
The phase the floor of 74.5 milliseconds costs is divided by the ninety degrees an integrator leaves, at crossover frequencies of three and six radians per second that the article assumes.

$$
\frac{\omega_{co} \tau_e}{\pi / 2} , \qquad \frac{3 \times 0.0745}{1.5708} = 0.1423 , \qquad \frac{6 \times 0.0745}{1.5708} = 0.2846
\tag{51}
$$

**Equation 52, Crossover at Which the Phase Margin Vanishes.**
Setting the phase margin of the crossover model to zero gives the highest crossover frequency the delay allows.

$$
\varphi_m = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \omega_{co} = \frac{\pi}{2 \tau_e}
\tag{52}
$$

**Equation 53, Invariance of an Ordinal Scale.**
An ordinal scale is one whose order survives every strictly increasing relabelling of its points.

$$
r_1 < r_2 \; \iff \; g \left( r_1 \right) < g \left( r_2 \right) \qquad \text{for every strictly increasing } g
\tag{53}
$$

**Equation 54, Median Commutes With Relabelling and the Mean Does Not.**
The median of relabelled ratings is the relabelled median, while the mean of relabelled ratings is in general not the relabelled mean.

$$
\operatorname{med} \left( g \left( r \right) \right) = g \left( \operatorname{med} \left( r \right) \right) , \qquad \operatorname{mean} \left( g \left( r \right) \right) \ne g \left( \operatorname{mean} \left( r \right) \right)
\tag{54}
$$

**Equation 55, Closed Loop Equals the Model When the Projector Vanishes.**
When the projector is zero the closed-loop transfer function of the host is exactly that of the model, with the host's dynamics cancelled.

$$
\Pi = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad G_{cl} \left( s \right) = C \left( s I - A_m \right)^{-1} B_m = G_m \left( s \right)
\tag{55}
$$

### Notation

- $x$, the state vector of the host aeroplane, with $x_m$ that of the model being simulated
- $u$, the control vector of the host aeroplane, with $u_m$ that of the model
- $A$, the dynamics matrix of the host aeroplane
- $A_m$, the dynamics matrix of the model being simulated
- $B$, the control effectiveness matrix of the host aeroplane
- $B_m$, the control effectiveness matrix of the model being simulated
- $K_x$, the feedback gain matrix on the host's own state
- $K_m$, the gain matrix on the model's state
- $K_u$, the gain matrix on the model's control input
- $B^{+}$, the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of the control effectiveness matrix
- $\Pi$, the orthogonal projector onto the subspace no combination of the host's controls can reach
- $\Delta A$, the change of dynamics the simulation demands
- $E$, the unmatchable residual of the demanded change
- $e_\infty$, the steady model-following error left by a residual no gain removes
- $C$, the output matrix, selecting what the pilot is given to feel
- $Z_\alpha$, the normal force derivative with respect to angle of attack
- $M_\alpha$, the pitching moment derivative with respect to angle of attack
- $M_q$, the pitching moment derivative with respect to pitch rate
- $\omega_n$, the undamped natural frequency of a second-order pair
- $\zeta$, the damping ratio
- $\lambda$, the eigenvalue of a dynamics matrix
- $t_2$, the time for a divergence to double in amplitude
- $\eta_\alpha$, the fraction of the angle-of-attack row's demanded change that no control law can produce, with $\eta_q$ that of the pitch-rate row
- $n_z$, the normal load factor
- $\bar{q}$, the dynamic pressure
- $C_{L_\alpha}$, the lift-curve slope per radian
- $\ell_f$, the distance of the flap's centre of pressure aft of the centre of gravity, with $\ell_h$ that of the horizontal tail
- $\bar{c}$, the mean aerodynamic chord
- $\kappa$, the condition number of a matrix
- $\sigma_{\min}$, the smallest singular value of a matrix
- $\gamma_s$, the symmetric tail deflection per unit angle of attack, with $\gamma_f$ that of the flap
- $\alpha_{\text{sat}}$, the angle of attack at which a surface reaches its deflection limit
- $\delta_{\max}$, the deflection limit of a control surface
- $R$, the rate limit of a control surface actuator
- $\hat{\delta}$, the amplitude of a sinusoidal surface deflection
- $\omega_c$, the full-deflection corner frequency of a surface
- $\omega_{sp}$, the short-period natural frequency
- $\delta_l$, the leading-edge flap deflection
- $\omega_p$, the pole of the published leading-edge flap schedule
- $P_s$, the static pressure
- $\tau$, the first-order lag time constant of a surface actuator, with $\tau_l$ that of the leading-edge flap
- $\tau_s$, the equivalent time delay of the simulated aeroplane as the pilot meets it
- $f_s$, the frame rate of the digital implementation
- $\tau_e$, the equivalent time delay of a cascade as the pilot meets it
- $\hat{\delta}_o$, the amplitude of the triangular output of a saturated rate limiter
- $N$, the describing function of a nonlinear element
- $Y_p$, the describing function of the human pilot, with $Y_c$ the transfer function of the controlled element
- $\omega_{co}$, the crossover frequency of the pilot and vehicle loop
- $\varphi_m$, the phase margin
- $g$, a strictly increasing map of the rating scale onto itself
- $\rho_p$, the share of the whole record's obligation that one contractor carries
- $V_{\text{all}}$, the obligation summed over the whole record
- $F$, the fraction of its flying life the aeroplane has carried an X number
- $T_n$, the date of the article, with $T_d$ the designation date and $T_0$ the first flight
- $G_{cl}$, the closed-loop transfer function of the host under model following, with $G_m$ that of the model
